lessons.title: Meaning of Features
lessons.summary: What a feature is and why it is the bridge between real-world data and a machine-learning model. Covers the core definition, the difference between features, observations, feature values, and the target, identifying feature columns in a dataset, the feature vector (x) and feature matrix (X), common feature forms (numerical, categorical, binary, ordinal, text, image, time), real-world task examples, the feature space, what makes a feature useful, raw data vs derived features, common misunderstandings, and a student pass/fail worked example.

content.text: What a model actually sees

A machine-learning model never sees a house, an email, or a patient — it only sees numbers describing them. Those descriptive pieces of information are called features, and they are the bridge between the messy real world and a model that can learn patterns. Getting features right is where most of the real work in machine learning happens.

content.caption: Figure 1. Features are the measurable inputs that connect real-world data to a model: raw object → features → ML model → prediction.

content.text: An individual measurable property, characteristic, attribute, or input variable used by a machine-learning model to describe an observation.

These notes focus on the meaning of features — their role as model inputs, their place in a dataset, their basic forms, and practical examples. Feature selection and transformation come in later sub-modules.

content.text: What is a feature?

In simple words, a feature is a piece of information that helps the model understand an item and make a prediction. When predicting a house price, the floor area, number of bedrooms, age of the house, and location score can all be features.
In a dataset, features usually appear as input columns. Each row is one observation, while each feature column records one property of that observation.

rows: One item or case being studied
A measurable input describing the item
The recorded value of a feature
The answer the model learns to predict
A collection of observations and variables

content.text: Columns describe; rows represent; the target is predicted.
content.title: Memory rule

content.caption: Figure 2. A house is one observation; its measurable properties — floor area 180 m², 3 bedrooms, age 8 years, location score 9/10, parking yes — are its features.

content.text: Features, observations, and target

items: Features are the inputs provided to the model.
An observation is one complete row or example.
The target is the output or answer the model is expected to predict.

content.text: Identifying features in a dataset
Consider this small house-price dataset. The first four columns are features and the final column is the target:
For House B, the feature values are 180, 3, 8, and 9.0. Together they describe the house to the model. Its price is not an input here — it is the target the model tries to learn.

content.caption: Figure 3. The same data as a feature matrix: rows are observations (House A–D) and columns are features (area, bedrooms, age, location score).

content.text: Feature vector and feature matrix
The ordered collection of all feature values for one observation, commonly written as x.
For House B: x = [180, 3, 8, 9.0]. The order matters because each position represents a particular feature.
content.title: Example feature vector

content.text: The feature vectors of many observations stacked together, commonly written as X — rows are observations and columns are features.

content.expression: X = all input data,   x = one observation's feature vector,   y = the target value or column
content.explanation: Capital X is the whole feature matrix; lowercase x is a single observation's vector; y is what the model predicts.

content.text: Common forms of features
A feature can store different forms of information. The form affects how the value is understood, but it remains a feature because it describes an observation.
The real-world property and its computer representation are related but different. “City” is a feature concept; “Karachi” is one feature value; a numerical encoding may later be used by the model.
content.title: Important distinction

content.text: Real-world examples

rows: Word count, suspicious phrases, sender domain, links
Pixel values or learned visual patterns

content.text: Feature space

A feature space is the coordinate space formed by the features. With two numerical features, each observation is a point on a 2-D graph; with more features the idea is the same even though it becomes hard to draw.

content.caption: Figure 4. A feature space with two features (age and income): each axis is one feature and each dot is one observation (one person).

content.text: Machine-learning models learn patterns from the position, distance, direction, or separation of observations in the feature space.
content.title: Why this matters

content.text: What makes information a useful feature?
A property is especially useful as a feature when it provides meaningful information about the problem. Useful features are usually:

items: Relevant — connected to the prediction task.
Measurable — recorded consistently for observations.
Available — obtainable when the model must make a prediction.
Clear — defined so that its meaning is not ambiguous.
Comparable — represented consistently across observations.

content.text: For house-price prediction, floor area is relevant and measurable. The owner's favourite colour may be recorded, but it is unlikely to explain the price and may not be a useful feature.
content.title: Example

content.text: Raw data versus features

Raw data are the original observations collected from the real world. Features are the specific pieces of information supplied to a model. Sometimes raw data already contain direct features; in other cases meaningful features must be derived from the raw data.
A feature is defined by its role as a model input, not only by its data type. A number, category, word pattern, or image measurement can all function as features.
content.title: Keep the concept clear

content.text: Common misunderstandings

rows: Every dataset column is a feature.
Some columns are targets, identifiers, notes, or metadata — not model inputs.
Features can start as categories, text, images, or dates (though many models need numeric form).
A feature and a feature value are the same.
A feature is the property (age); a feature value is the recorded value (32).
More features always produce a better model.
Irrelevant or misleading inputs can reduce model quality.
The target is also an input feature.
In supervised learning, the target is the output the model learns to predict.

content.text: Worked example: predicting student pass/fail
A model must predict whether a student will pass a course.

items: Identify the observation — one student is one observation.
Identify possible features — attendance %, average quiz score, weekly study hours, submitted assignments.
Identify the target — pass or fail.
Write one feature vector — for Student A, x = [88, 74, 6, 9].
Interpret the role of features — the model compares feature patterns across many students and learns how those inputs relate to the pass/fail target.

content.text: x = [88, 74, 6, 9] means 88% attendance, a 74 average quiz score, 6 study hours per week, and 9 submitted assignments.

keyPoints: A feature is a measurable input property that describes an observation to a model — defined by its role as an input, not only by its data type.
Distinguish the pieces: a feature is the property, a feature value is its recorded value, an observation is one row, and the target is what the model predicts.
One observation's ordered feature values form a feature vector (x); stacking many gives the feature matrix (X), with the target column y.

Treating the target as an input feature in supervised learning.

lessons.title: Why Feature Engineering Matters
lessons.summary: Why the representation of data — not just the algorithm — often decides whether a model succeeds. Covers the core definition of feature engineering and eight concrete reasons it matters (exposing hidden patterns, improving performance, making raw data usable, reducing noise, simplifying the model, improving interpretability, supporting robustness, and encoding domain knowledge), a house-price worked example, an illustrative accuracy comparison, the x → x² transformation that turns a curve into a line, examples across data types, good-vs-poor features, the risks (leakage, overfitting, inconsistent processing), and a customer-churn mini case study.

content.text: Why the same data can succeed or fail

Two teams can start with exactly the same raw data and the same algorithm, yet get very different results. The difference is often not the model — it is how the data was represented. A model never understands what a house, a date, or an email really is; it only learns from the numeric features it is given. Shaping those features well is what feature engineering is about, and it is frequently the single biggest lever on model quality.

content.caption: Figure 1. Feature engineering is the bridge that turns raw data into useful model inputs: raw data → feature engineering → useful features → ML model → better output.

content.text: The process of creating, transforming, combining, representing, or selecting input variables so that a machine-learning model can learn useful patterns more effectively.

These notes focus on why feature engineering matters. The step-by-step methods for encoding, scaling, selection, extraction, and interactions belong to later sub-modules — here they appear only when needed to explain their importance.
content.title: Scope

content.text: What you'll be able to do

items: Define feature engineering and explain its purpose.
Describe how good features improve learning, performance, efficiency, interpretability, and robustness.
Recognise when raw data does not directly show the pattern a model needs.
Distinguish raw features, engineered features, and irrelevant features.
Interpret simple examples and charts showing the effect of feature engineering.

content.text: A model learns from representations, not from reality. It cannot see the meaning behind raw data — only the numeric or encoded features supplied to it. Better representations usually lead to better learning.
content.title: Key idea

content.text: Eight reasons it matters
1. It exposes hidden patterns
Raw variables may hold useful information, but the relationship can be hard for a model to detect. Transforming or combining variables can reveal a simpler, more learnable pattern.
2. It improves predictive performance
Relevant, informative features help the model separate classes or estimate values more accurately. Poorly represented data can cap performance even when a powerful algorithm is used.
3. It makes raw data usable

Dates, text, categories, images, and measurements are not always directly suitable for an algorithm. Feature engineering converts them into meaningful numeric inputs such as weekday, word frequency, one-hot indicators, or normalized measurements.
4. It reduces noise and irrelevant information
Removing or avoiding weak features can stop the model from fitting accidental patterns, which improves generalization to new, unseen data.
5. It can simplify the model
A clear feature representation may let a simpler algorithm perform well. Simpler models are often faster to train, easier to explain, and easier to maintain.
6. It improves interpretability
Meaningful features such as debt-to-income ratio or customer tenure are easier to explain than thousands of unprocessed values. This helps people understand why a prediction was made.
7. It supports robustness and consistency
Scaling, grouping, and domain-based features reduce sensitivity to units, outliers, or small input changes — making the model more stable in practical use.
8. It brings domain knowledge into the model
Knowledge from finance, healthcare, marketing, or engineering can be encoded through useful ratios, trends, and interactions, giving the model variables closer to the real process being studied.

rows: Can improve accuracy and reduce error
May cut complexity and training time
Connects the model to real-world logic

content.text: Worked example: house-price prediction
Suppose a dataset contains these raw columns:

items: Date of sale
Year built
Living area
Number of bedrooms
Sale price (target)

content.text: None of these is wrong, but a few engineered features describe the price far more directly:

items: House age = year of sale − year built
Space-per-bedroom ratio = living area ÷ number of bedrooms
Sale season = winter, spring, summer, or autumn, derived from the date

rows: Age relates to condition more directly than the raw year.
Shows how spacious the house is relative to room count.

content.text: The new features do not invent facts from nowhere. They reorganize existing information into forms more directly connected to the prediction task.
content.title: Interpretation

content.text: The effect on model performance

The chart below is a simple illustration of how a more informative feature set can lift validation performance. The values are illustrative, not a guaranteed result — the real gain depends on the dataset and model.

content.caption: Figure 2. Illustrative validation accuracy: raw features 72% vs engineered features 88%. The exact numbers vary; the direction is the point.

content.text: How a transformation reveals a pattern

Consider a target that depends roughly on the square of an input. A model that only receives the raw input x sees a curved (U-shaped) relationship that a straight line cannot fit. Creating the feature x² turns that relationship into an almost straight line — which a simple linear model learns easily.
Before: only the raw feature x

content.caption: Figure 3. With the raw feature x, the target follows a curved U-shape that a straight line cannot capture.

content.text: After: adding the engineered feature x²

content.caption: Figure 4. Plotted against the engineered feature x², the same data becomes an almost straight line — easy for a simple model to fit.

content.text: Same data, same target — only the representation changed. Feature engineering did not add information; it made the existing pattern visible to a simple model.
content.title: The takeaway

content.text: Examples across different data types
The value of feature engineering shows up in every kind of data — not just tables of numbers.

rows: Combines two measurements into one indicator.

content.text: Good features vs poor features
More columns is not the goal — useful signal is. A feature is only helpful if it adds relevant, stable, honestly-available information.

rows: Changes unpredictably or needs unavailable data
Uses incompatible units or raw categories

content.text: Powerful, but it must be done carefully
Feature engineering can help a great deal — and it can also quietly harm a model if done without discipline. Watch for these traps:
Data leakage — a feature must not use information that would be unavailable at the moment the prediction is made. Leaked features look brilliant in testing and fail in production.
content.title: Leakage

items: Overfitting — too many highly specific features let the model memorize the training data instead of learning the pattern.
Wrong assumptions — a transformation based on incorrect domain knowledge can reduce performance.
Inconsistent processing — the same transformations must be applied to training, validation, test, and future production data.
Unnecessary complexity — more features are not automatically better; useful signal matters more than quantity.

content.text: Mini case study: customer churn

A company wants to predict whether a customer will stop using its service. The raw data contains signup date, last login date, number of support complaints, and monthly usage. On their own these raw fields are only loosely tied to churn — but a few engineered features make the risk far clearer:

rows: Long-term and new customers behave differently.
A long inactive period may signal churn risk.
A ratio makes complaint frequency comparable across customers.
A falling trend can be an early warning signal.

content.text: Quick recap

rows: Why can raw data be insufficient?
It may be unstructured, poorly scaled, or only indirectly related to the target.
To present information in a form that helps the model learn the real pattern.
No — it may transform, combine, encode, select, or remove features.
Can it improve a simple model?
Yes — better inputs can let a simple model perform strongly.
Using leaked, unstable, or misleading features.

content.text: Feature engineering matters because models learn from representations — and a meaningful representation can make patterns clearer, predictions stronger, models simpler, and results easier to explain.
content.title: One-sentence summary

content.text: Self-check

1. Why does a machine-learning model depend so heavily on the quality of its input features? 2. How can feature engineering reveal a hidden pattern? 3. Give one example of converting a date into useful features. 4. Why might a simpler model perform well after feature engineering? 5. What is data leakage, and why is it dangerous?
content.title: Test yourself

content.text: Answers

items: The model only learns from the features it is given; if they represent the pattern poorly, even a strong algorithm is limited.
By transforming or combining raw variables so a hidden relationship becomes a simpler, more learnable one (e.g. x → x²).
A sale date can become weekday, month, or season — e.g. 15 July → summer.
Good features make the underlying pattern almost linear or clearly separable, so a simple model can capture it.
Using information that would not be available at prediction time (or that leaks the target); it inflates test scores and then fails in real use.

keyPoints: A model learns only from the features it is given, so the representation of the data often matters as much as the algorithm.
Good feature engineering exposes hidden patterns, improves accuracy, makes raw data (dates, text, categories) usable, reduces noise, and can simplify the model.
It also improves interpretability, supports robustness/consistency, and encodes domain knowledge through ratios, trends, and interactions.
The same data plotted against an engineered feature (e.g. x² instead of x) can turn an unlearnable curve into an easy straight line — without adding information.
It must be done carefully: data leakage, overfitting, wrong assumptions, and inconsistent processing can all silently harm a model.
commonMistakes: Assuming a more powerful algorithm can always compensate for poorly represented data.
Believing feature engineering always means adding more columns rather than transforming or selecting.
Creating a feature that uses information unavailable at prediction time (data leakage).
Applying transformations inconsistently across training, validation, test, and production data.

lessons.title: Creating New Features
lessons.summary: How to derive fresh, more informative input variables from the columns you already have. Covers the definition of feature creation and why it helps, then the six main methods — mathematical combinations, interaction features, date/time decomposition, aggregation, binning/grouping, and domain-based features (plus text-derived features) — an online-store worked example, a pandas implementation, a six-point usefulness checklist, common mistakes (especially target leakage), a safe creation workflow, quick revision, and a delivery-dataset practice activity.

content.text: Turning columns you have into columns you need

A dataset rarely arrives with the exact columns a model needs. The information is usually there — but locked inside raw fields like a date, a price, and a quantity. Creating new features is the craft of deriving fresh input variables from the columns you already have, so a pattern that was hidden becomes something the model can read directly. Think of it as a small factory: raw columns go in, clearer signals come out.

content.caption: Figure 1. Feature creation as a “feature factory”: raw columns (date, price, quantity, length, width) are transformed into more informative inputs (month, total cost, area, price/unit, weekend flag).

content.text: Deriving additional input variables from existing data so that a machine-learning model can recognise patterns more easily. The derived variables are often called engineered features.
These notes focus on creating new features. Feature selection, scaling, encoding, and dimensionality reduction appear only where needed for context — they are covered in later sub-modules.
content.title: Scope

content.text: What you'll be able to do

items: Define feature creation and explain its role.
Create mathematical, interaction, date/time, aggregation, binning, and domain-based features.
Recognise useful features and avoid target leakage or meaningless combinations.
Apply feature creation in a small pandas example and judge whether the new features help.

content.text: A raw column may hold the right information in a form that is hard for a model to use. A new feature expresses that same information in a clearer, more useful form.
content.title: The simple idea

content.text: Why create new features?

items: Reveal hidden relationships — a ratio, total, or interaction may relate to the target more closely than either raw column alone.
Represent domain knowledge — a feature can express how the real-world process actually works.
Simplify the learning problem — a model learns faster when useful patterns are stated directly.
Improve predictive performance — relevant features can raise validation accuracy or cut error.
Make results interpretable — features like age, total spend, or average order value make sense to people.

content.caption: Figure 2. Illustrative validation accuracy: raw features 72% → new features added 82% → useful features validated 86%. Example values — real gains depend on the dataset and model.

content.text: More features do not automatically mean a better model. A new feature is valuable only when it is logically valid and improves generalisation on unseen data.
content.title: Important

content.text: Six main ways to create features
1. Mathematical combinations
Combine two or more numeric columns with arithmetic:

items: Sum — total_items = item_A + item_B + item_C
Difference — profit = selling_price − cost_price
Product — area = length × width
Ratio — price_per_unit = total_price ÷ quantity
Percentage — discount_rate = discount ÷ original_price × 100

rows: Captures combined size of an object
Turns a date into a meaningful number

content.text: When creating ratios, guard against division by zero and check whether very small denominators produce extreme values.
content.title: Division safety

content.text: 2. Interaction features

An interaction feature represents the combined effect of two variables — for example area = length × width. The interaction can reveal information that is weak or incomplete in each feature on its own.

content.caption: Figure 3. Length alone relates only loosely to price (left); the engineered feature area = length × width shows a much stronger, cleaner relationship with the target (right).

content.text: 3. Date and time features
A single date or timestamp can be decomposed into several features that capture calendar or time patterns:

items: Year, quarter, month, and day
Day of week, or a weekend flag
Hour of day, or a time-of-day group
Elapsed time, such as account_age_days
Season, public-holiday flag, or business-hours flag when relevant

content.caption: Figure 4. One timestamp (2026-08-04 13:30) generates several useful features: year 2026, month 8, day 4, weekday Tuesday, hour 13.

content.text: 4. Aggregation features
Aggregation summarises multiple records that belong to the same customer, product, device, or time period into one representative value.
5. Binned or grouped features
Binning converts a continuous variable into meaningful groups — useful when thresholds matter or for interpretability.
Binning improves interpretability and can capture thresholds, but it also discards numeric detail. Choose boundaries using domain knowledge or data analysis, not arbitrarily.
content.title: Trade-off

content.text: 6. Domain-based features
Domain-based features use subject knowledge to encode real-world meaning — often the most powerful kind:

items: Healthcare — body mass index = weight ÷ height²
Finance — debt-to-income ratio = debt ÷ income
Retail — average order value = total spend ÷ number of orders
Manufacturing — defect rate = defective units ÷ total units
Transport — average speed = distance ÷ travel time

content.text: A feature built on correct domain knowledge is usually more useful than a random mathematical combination.
content.title: Best practice

content.text: Bonus: text-derived features
Simple numeric features can be pulled from text even before advanced text representation is applied:

items: Character count and word count
Number of capital letters, digits, or punctuation marks
Presence of a keyword or URL
Average word length
Count of positive, negative, or urgency-related terms

Suppose an online store has these raw columns (shown split across two tables so every column stays readable on a phone):
From these raw columns we can create several new features:

rows: day of week is Sat or Sun
Current value relative to customer activity

content.text: Creating features in pandas
The same feature types — mathematical, date/time, binned, and a safe ratio — translate directly into a few lines of pandas:

content.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# Mathematical feature
df["total_value"] = df["unit_price"] * df["quantity"]

# Date/time features
df["order_date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["order_date"])
df["order_month"] = df["order_date"].dt.month
df["is_weekend"] = df["order_date"].dt.dayofweek >= 5

# Binned feature
df["age_group"] = pd.cut(
    df["customer_age"],
    bins=[0, 24, 44, 64, np.inf],
    labels=["18-24", "25-44", "45-64", "65+"],
)

# Safe ratio feature (avoids division by zero)
df["price_per_item"] = np.where(
    df["quantity"] > 0,
    df["total_value"] / df["quantity"],
    np.nan,
)
content.explanation: Each block builds one feature type; the np.where guard keeps ratio features finite when the denominator is zero.

content.text: Create the feature using the training-data logic, then apply exactly the same transformation to validation, test, and future data. Inconsistent processing silently breaks the model in production.
content.title: Coding principle

content.text: Is a new feature actually useful?
Before trusting a new feature, run it through six quick checks:

items: Logic check — does the feature have a valid real-world meaning?
Data-quality check — does it create missing, infinite, or extreme values?
Leakage check — does it use information unavailable at prediction time?
Relationship check — does it show a useful association with the target or improve class separation?
Validation check — does cross-validation or a holdout set improve after adding it?
Stability check — can it be calculated reliably for future observations?

content.text: Common mistakes to avoid

Target leakage — creating a feature from the answer, or from information that only becomes available after the prediction event. For predicting loan default, “number of missed payments after approval” must not be used: it happens after the decision.
content.title: The biggest trap

items: Random combinations — multiplying or dividing columns without a meaningful hypothesis.
Division by zero — producing infinite values in ratio features.
Too many features — hundreds of noisy variables increase overfitting and computation.
Inconsistent processing — creating features differently in training and test data.
Ignoring missing values — letting a transformation create extra missing or invalid observations.
Using identifiers as quantities — treating order ID, phone number, or customer number as measurements.

content.text: A safe feature-creation workflow

content.caption: Figure 5. A safe workflow: Raw Data → Understand → Create → Validate → Model.

items: Start from the prediction goal and know what information is available at prediction time.
Study the meaning and distribution of the existing columns.
Propose features using domain knowledge and observed patterns.
Create features in a reproducible transformation pipeline.
Check quality, leakage, and extreme values.
Compare model performance using a proper validation method.
Keep features that are useful, stable, and explainable.

content.text: Quick revision

rows: Deriving additional model inputs from existing data.
Mathematical, interaction, date/time, aggregation, binning, text-derived, domain-based.
Express useful patterns more clearly for the model.
Features must be logical, available at prediction time, and validated on unseen data.
Target leakage and overfitting from noisy or excessive features.
Compare the same model before and after adding the feature, on validation data.

content.text: Good feature creation turns raw data into meaningful signals. The best new features are logical, reproducible, leakage-free, and proven useful on validation data.
content.title: Final takeaway

content.text: Mini practice activity
A delivery dataset contains: order_time, dispatch_time, distance_km, fuel_used_litres, item_weight_kg, and delivery_status.

items: Create delivery_time_minutes from dispatch_time and order_time.
Create fuel_efficiency = distance_km ÷ fuel_used_litres.
Create weight_per_km = item_weight_kg ÷ distance_km.
Create an is_peak_hour flag from order_time.
Explain which features could help predict whether a delivery will be late.

content.text: Which of your new features are safe to use for predicting lateness before the delivery finishes — and which one would be leakage?
content.title: Think it through

content.text: Answer

fuel_efficiency, weight_per_km, and is_peak_hour are safe — they are known before or independently of the outcome. delivery_time_minutes is leakage if the goal is to predict lateness before the delivery is completed, because it can only be measured once the delivery has already happened.

keyPoints: Creating new features means deriving additional input variables from existing data so patterns become easier for a model to learn.
The main methods are mathematical combinations, interaction features, date/time decomposition, aggregation, binning/grouping, and domain-based features (plus simple text-derived features).
A new feature is only valuable if it is logical, available at prediction time, stable, and shown to improve performance on unseen (validation) data.
Guard against division by zero, and apply exactly the same transformation to training, validation, test, and future data.
The biggest risk is target leakage — building a feature from the answer or from information that only exists after the prediction moment.
commonMistakes: Target leakage: creating a feature from the answer or from post-event information.
Combining columns randomly without a meaningful hypothesis, or creating too many noisy features.
Producing infinite/extreme values by dividing by zero or tiny denominators.
Creating features inconsistently across training and test data, or treating identifiers (order ID, phone number) as quantities.

lessons.title: Transforming Existing Features
lessons.summary: How to reshape the values already in your dataset so a model can use them better. Covers the definition of feature transformation (x' = f(x)) and why scale, skewness, non-linearity, and extreme values matter, then five method families — scaling/rescaling (min-max, standardization, robust), distribution transforms (log/sqrt/power, log1p), binning, polynomial and interaction terms, and clipping/capping/winsorization — how to choose a transformation, leakage-safe fitting (split first, fit on training only) with a scikit-learn example, a customer-spending case study, common mistakes, quick revision, and self-check.

content.text: Reshaping the values you already have

Sometimes the right feature is already in your dataset — it is just in an awkward shape. Incomes span from hundreds to millions, ages sit on a different scale than test scores, and a handful of extreme values drown out everything else. Feature transformation is the craft of applying a mathematical or rule-based function to an existing feature so its values become easier, safer, and more meaningful for a model — without collecting anything new.

content.caption: Figure 1. A safe transformation workflow: original feature → choose a transformation → fit using training data → model-ready transformed feature. The same fitted transformation is then applied to validation, test, and future data.

content.text: Applying a mathematical or rule-based function to an existing input feature so that its values become more useful for a machine-learning model. If x is the original feature, the transformed feature is x' = f(x).

These notes focus on transforming values already present in a dataset — scaling, distribution transforms, binning, polynomial/interaction terms, and outlier capping. Feature selection, missing-value imputation, and full categorical encoding belong to other sub-modules.
content.title: Scope

content.text: A transformation changes the representation of a feature; it does not change the real-world observation. A customer earning 150,000 is the same customer — the model just receives a different numerical representation. Transforming a feature is not the same as changing the target variable.
content.title: Key distinction

content.text: What you'll be able to do

items: Define feature transformation and distinguish it from changing the target.
Explain why scale, skewness, non-linearity, and extreme values matter.
Apply standardization, min-max scaling, log transformation, and binning.
Select a transformation based on the feature's distribution and the model.
Avoid data leakage by fitting transformations on training data only.

content.text: Why transform existing features?
A good transformation targets a specific, observed problem in the data and improves one or more of these:

items: Numerical stability — very large or tiny values are less likely to cause optimization problems.
Learning speed — gradient-based algorithms converge faster when features are on similar scales.
Model fit — a transformed feature can show a simpler, more learnable relationship with the target.
Interpretability — bins or standardized scores make values easier to compare.

rows: KNN, SVM, k-means, neural nets, regularized regression

content.text: Method 1 · Scaling and rescaling
Scaling changes the numerical range or centre of a feature while preserving the ordering of observations — the biggest value stays the biggest, it just lives on a new scale.

content.caption: Figure 2. Min-max and z-score scaling both shrink the magnitude of the original values, but every observation keeps the same relative order.

rows: A fixed range like 0–1 is useful
Output is not a fixed range
Record the unit to avoid confusion

content.text: Worked example: min-max scaling
Suppose the training ages are 20, 30, 40, 50, and 60. To scale age 40:

content.explanation: The minimum (20) maps to 0, the maximum (60) maps to 1, and 40 sits exactly halfway at 0.50.

content.text: Decision trees, random forests, and gradient-boosted trees split on thresholds, so they are largely insensitive to feature scale. You may still scale for pipeline consistency, but it usually does not improve these models.
content.title: When scaling is unnecessary

content.text: Method 2 · Distribution transformations
Distribution transformations change the shape of a numerical feature — usually to reduce skewness, compress large values, or make the relationship with the target easier to model.

content.caption: Figure 3. A strongly right-skewed feature (left) becomes far more balanced after a log1p transformation (right), which compresses the long tail of extreme values.

rows: Positive values with an inverse relation

content.text: log1p(x) means log(1 + x). It safely transforms zero values, whereas log(0) is undefined. Negative values still need another strategy, such as Yeo-Johnson or a justified shift.
content.title: Why log1p is common

content.text: A small numerical example
Multiplying the original value by 10 adds only about 2.30 to the transformed value each time. That is exactly why the transformation reduces the dominance of very large observations.
Method 3 · Binning (discretization)
Binning converts a continuous numerical feature into a small number of intervals or groups. The cut points must come from domain knowledge or a justified data-based rule — not guesswork.

content.caption: Figure 4. Example age bins: Child (0–18), Young adult (18–35), Middle adult (35–60), Older adult (60–100).

rows: Each interval has the same width
Some bins may be nearly empty
Each bin holds a similar count

content.text: Binning reduces noise and aids explanation, but it discards detail. Ages 36 and 59 become identical if both land in the same “middle adult” bin. Compare binned and continuous versions on validation before committing.
content.title: Trade-off

content.text: Method 4 · Polynomial and interaction terms

Polynomial transformations create powers of a feature (x², x³); interaction transformations multiply features (x1 × x2) to represent combined effects. Both let a linear model describe non-linear structure.

content.caption: Figure 5. A straight-line fit using x alone (dashed) misses the curve; adding an x² term lets the same linear model follow the U-shaped pattern (solid).

rows: A curved effect that grows with size
A more flexible S-shaped or asymmetric curve
Advertising's effect may change by season

content.text: Higher-degree polynomial terms can overfit, become highly correlated, and produce very large values. Use low degrees plus cross-validation and regularization unless strong domain knowledge justifies more complexity.
content.title: Control complexity

content.text: Method 5 · Clipping, capping, and winsorization
Capping limits extremely small or large values to chosen thresholds. Winsorization is a common form that replaces values beyond chosen percentiles with the percentile boundary.
Do not cap a value just because it is unusual. First check whether it is a data error, a valid rare case, or an important signal. Unjustified capping can hide meaningful risk or fraud patterns.
content.title: Use only with justification

content.text: Choosing the right transformation
Match the transformation to the problem you actually see in the data:

rows: A linear model misses a curve

content.text: A practical decision process:

items: Inspect the feature with summary statistics, histograms, and box plots.
Identify the actual problem: scale, skewness, outliers, non-linearity, or interpretability.
Select the simplest transformation that addresses that problem.
Fit the transformation on training data only.
Evaluate the full pipeline using cross-validation or a validation set.
Keep it only if it improves performance, stability, or justified interpretability.

content.text: Preventing data leakage

Many transformations learn values from data — the mean and standard deviation for standardization, the min and max for min-max scaling, quantile cut points, and power-transform parameters. If those are learned from the whole dataset, information from the test set leaks into training.
Split the data first. Fit the transformation on the training set only. Then use those learned parameters to transform the validation set, test set, and future observations.
content.title: The correct rule

rows: Scale the whole dataset, then split
Split first, fit scaler on training, transform all sets
Learn bin thresholds from training data only
Compare transforms on the final test set
Use CV/validation; reserve test for final evaluation

content.text: Leakage-safe Python example
This illustrates leakage-safe log transformation and scaling — split first, then fit on training data only:

content.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

# X contains two columns: income and age
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.20, random_state=42
)

# 1) Distribution transform for a right-skewed positive feature
X_train = X_train.copy()
X_test = X_test.copy()
X_train["income"] = np.log1p(X_train["income"])
X_test["income"] = np.log1p(X_test["income"])

# 2) Fit the scaler on training data ONLY
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_train_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_scaled = scaler.transform(X_test)   # transform, not fit
content.explanation: log1p is applied element-wise (safe per row), but the scaler is fit only on training data and merely transforms the test data.

content.text: In real projects, use a scikit-learn Pipeline or ColumnTransformer so fitting, transformation, and prediction stay consistent during cross-validation and deployment.

content.text: Mini case study: customer spending
A retailer has a feature annual_spending. Most customers spend between 500 and 5,000, but a few corporate customers spend above 100,000 — so the raw distribution is heavily right-skewed.

rows: Store fitted preprocessing in the pipeline

content.text: After the log transform, a change from 1,000 to 2,000 is treated much like a proportional change from 10,000 to 20,000 — sensible when relative differences matter more than absolute ones.
Common mistakes and corrections

Scale when the model/data justify it
Use log1p for zeros; power transform for negatives
Fitting the transform before the split
Compare binned vs continuous on validation

content.text: Quick revision

Transforming existing features means converting raw feature values into a representation that is easier, safer, or more meaningful for a model — and it is valuable only when it is mathematically valid, appropriate for the model, consistently applied, and confirmed by evaluation.
content.title: In one sentence

items: Transform to solve a specific, observed problem — not just because a technique exists.
The best transformation depends on both the feature distribution and the chosen model.
Preserve interpretability and real-world meaning whenever possible.
Fit data-dependent transformations on training data only.
Evaluate the transformation as part of the complete ML pipeline.

It compresses the long right tail so large values stop dominating and the pattern becomes easier to model.

keyPoints: Feature transformation applies a function x' = f(x) to an existing feature to make its values easier, safer, or more meaningful — it changes representation, not the real observation.
Scaling (min-max, standardization, robust) puts features on comparable scales and speeds up distance- and gradient-based models; tree models rarely need it.

Distribution transforms (log/log1p, sqrt, power) reduce skewness and compress large values; binning groups continuous values; polynomial/interaction terms let linear models fit curves and combined effects.

lessons.title: Interaction Features
lessons.summary: How to capture the combined effect of two or more variables when their influence is not independent. Covers the definition of an interaction feature and the main-effects vs interaction model (adding a b3·X1×X2 term), the house-area×location intuition, recognising interactions from non-parallel lines, the three interaction types (numeric×numeric, numeric×categorical, categorical×categorical) plus higher-order terms, the multiplicative interaction surface, a purchase-prediction worked example, pandas and scikit-learn PolynomialFeatures code, interpreting an interaction coefficient (the slope of X1 becomes 2+0.5·X2), which models need explicit interactions, controlled validation, mean-centering, common mistakes, a workflow, and an electricity-consumption practice activity.

content.text: When two features only make sense together

Most models start by assuming each feature acts on its own: more area adds a fixed amount of value, a bigger discount adds a fixed amount of appeal, and the two never talk to each other. Reality is rarely so tidy. Extra square metres are worth far more in a premium neighbourhood, and a discount tempts a frequent visitor far more than a one-time browser. An interaction feature captures exactly this — the combined effect of two variables that a plain additive model would miss.

content.caption: Figure 1. The interaction-feature workflow: original features X1, X2 → create interaction X1 × X2 → train model with X1, X2, X1×X2 → evaluate validation score.

content.text: A new feature that represents the combined effect of two or more original features. It is useful when the effect of one feature on the target changes according to the value or category of another feature.
A model with only separate features assumes their effects are independent and additive. An interaction term lets the features influence each other.
content.title: Core idea

content.text: These notes stay focused on interaction features — how they are defined, created, interpreted, selected, validated, and used. Other transformation and selection topics live in their own sub-modules.
content.title: Scope

content.text: What you'll be able to do

items: Define an interaction feature in simple terms.
Explain why the effect of one feature may depend on another.
Create numerical×numerical, numerical×categorical, and categorical×categorical interactions.
Interpret interaction coefficients in a linear model.
Use interactions safely without leakage, excessive complexity, or overfitting.
Evaluate whether an interaction genuinely improves validation performance.

content.text: The maths, in one line
Compare a plain additive model with one that adds a product term:

content.expression:
Main-effects model:   y = b0 + b1·X1 + b2·X2
Interaction model:    y = b0 + b1·X1 + b2·X2 + b3·(X1 × X2)
content.explanation: The extra b3(X1 × X2) term is what lets the slope of one feature change with the other.

rows: Baseline prediction when X1 and X2 are zero.
Main effect of X1 when X2 = 0.
Main effect of X2 when X1 = 0.
Combined effect: how the slope of X1 changes as X2 changes.

content.text: Intuition: house area × location quality

A model predicts house price from area and location quality. A larger house usually costs more — but the price gained per square metre is much greater in a premium location. So area and location interact: their joint value is more than the sum of their separate effects.

content.caption: Figure 2. House area × location quality: the extra value of size is amplified when the location is also strong.

content.text: The last row — large area and strong location — has a far larger interaction value, helping the model represent the extra value created by that specific combination.
content.title: Interpretation

content.text: How to recognise an interaction
The classic visual sign is non-parallel lines when you plot the target against one feature, split by another. If the lines fan apart or cross, the effect of one feature depends on the other.

content.caption: Figure 3. Advertising has a much steeper effect under high seasonal demand than under low demand — the non-parallel lines reveal an interaction.

rows: Little or no interaction; one feature shifts the intercept, not the slope.
Interaction exists; the slope of one feature changes across levels of another.
Strong interaction; the direction of an effect may reverse.
Possible non-linear interaction or missing transformations.

content.text: The main types of interaction
Numerical × numerical
Multiply, divide, or otherwise combine two numeric variables when domain logic suggests a joint effect.

rows: Study time is more productive with stronger foundations.
Advertising returns more when demand is already strong.
Perceived heat depends on both together.
Repayment burden depends jointly on principal and rate.

content.text: Numerical × categorical
Multiply a numeric variable by a binary or one-hot category indicator — this gives each category its own slope.

rows: Return to experience may differ in Sales.
Premium customers may react differently to price.
Engine-size effect may differ by fuel type.

content.text: Categorical × categorical
Combine two categories into a joint category, or multiply their one-hot indicators.

rows: Behaviour may depend on the exact device–browser pair.
Regional demand may vary by product category.
Salary may depend on both education and occupation.

content.text: Higher-order interactions
A three-way term like X1 × X2 × X3 means the relationship between X1 and the target depends jointly on X2 and X3. These can be powerful but are hard to interpret and overfit quickly.
Begin with two-way interactions. Add three-way interactions only when strong domain knowledge and validation evidence support them.
content.title: Practical rule

content.text: The interaction surface
Multiplying two features creates a surface where the interaction is small if either feature is small, and large only when both are large — a genuinely joint effect, not a simple sum.

content.caption: Figure 4. Heatmap of a multiplicative interaction X1 × X2: the value stays low unless both features are high (bright top-right corner).

content.text: Worked example: predicting a purchase

Goal: predict whether a customer buys, using website visits and discount percentage. A discount may matter far more for customers who visit frequently. The tables below are split so every column stays readable on a phone:

Neither visits nor discount alone predicts the purchase — customers B and C have moderate values of one but not the other. Only when both are high (the large interaction values for D and E) does the purchase happen. That pattern is exactly what the product term captures.
A safe procedure for using it:

items: Start with the original columns: visits and discount.
Create the interaction: visits_discount = visits × discount.
Keep the two original features as well as the new interaction.
Split into training and validation sets before fitting preprocessing decisions.
Compare validation performance with and without the interaction.
Retain the feature only if it improves generalisation and makes domain sense.

content.text: Creating interactions in Python
Manual creation with pandas

content.code:
import pandas as pd

# Numerical × numerical interaction
df["visits_discount"] = df["website_visits"] * df["discount_pct"]

# Numerical × categorical interaction (is_premium must be 0 or 1)
df["price_premium"] = df["price"] * df["is_premium"]

# Categorical × categorical interaction
df["device_browser"] = (
    df["device_type"].astype(str) + "_" + df["browser"].astype(str)
)
content.explanation: Each line builds one interaction type: a product of numerics, a numeric times a 0/1 flag, and a joined category string.

content.text: Automatic interactions with scikit-learn

content.code:
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures

interaction_maker = PolynomialFeatures(
    degree=2,
    interaction_only=True,   # products only, no x^2 terms
    include_bias=False,
)

X_interactions = interaction_maker.fit_transform(X_numeric)
feature_names = interaction_maker.get_feature_names_out(X_numeric.columns)
content.explanation: interaction_only=True keeps cross-products (X1×X2) but drops pure powers; it can still produce many columns.

content.text: PolynomialFeatures can generate a large number of columns. Use it inside a pipeline and evaluate with cross-validation — do not generate every possible interaction blindly.
content.title: Important

content.text: Interpreting an interaction coefficient
Consider the fitted model y = 10 + 2·X1 + 3·X2 + 0.5·(X1 × X2). The effect of X1 is no longer a single number — it depends on X2:

rows: What is the effect of X1?
Not fixed — the slope of X1 equals 2 + 0.5·X2.
A one-unit rise in X1 increases y by 2 units.
A one-unit rise in X1 increases y by 2 + 0.5(4) = 4 units.
Each one-unit increase in X2 raises the slope of X1 by 0.5.

content.text: When an interaction is present, do not interpret a main-effect coefficient on its own. Always state the level of the other interacting variable.
content.title: Key interpretation rule

content.text: Which models need explicit interactions?
Some model families only learn additive effects and must be handed interaction terms; others discover them on their own.

rows: Learns additive effects unless product terms are added.
Log-odds are additive unless interactions are included.
Decision boundary is linear in the supplied features.
Conditional splits can behave like interactions.
Trees model interactions; good features can add efficiency.
Boosted trees discover complex interactions automatically.
Hidden layers learn interactions; engineered ones help with little data.

content.text: Does the interaction actually help?
Use a controlled comparison: same model, same data split, same preprocessing and metric. The only planned difference should be the interaction feature.

content.caption: Figure 5. Illustrative validation RMSE: 18.4 with main effects only vs 11.2 after adding a useful interaction (lower is better).

rows: Does the benefit hold across folds or repeated splits?
Can the combined effect be explained in domain terms?
Is the gain large enough to justify the extra feature?
Was it built only from information available at prediction time?
Does it behave sensibly for unusual or extreme values?

content.text: Centering before interactions
For linear models, centering numeric variables (subtracting their mean) makes coefficients easier to interpret and reduces multicollinearity between the main effects and the product term.

content.code:
# Mean-centering example
x1_centered = df["x1"] - df["x1"].mean()
x2_centered = df["x2"] - df["x2"].mean()
df["x1_x2_interaction"] = x1_centered * x2_centered
content.explanation: Centre each variable first, then multiply — the interaction is now measured around a meaningful reference point.

rows: b1 is the effect of X1 when X2 = 0.
b1 is the effect of X1 when X2 is at its mean.
The reference point is usually meaningful.
Product term may correlate strongly with main effects.
Correlation is reduced, improving numerical stability.

content.text: Common mistakes and risks

rows: Keep X1 and X2 when using X1 × X2, unless theory says otherwise.
Use domain knowledge, regularisation, and selection.
Use only variables known at prediction time.
Products of large values dominate optimisation.
Scale or centre numeric inputs when appropriate.
Very few examples give unstable estimates.
Merge rare categories or use regularised encodings.
A predictive interaction is not automatically causal.
Use causal methods for causal claims.

content.text: Recommended workflow

items: Understand the domain — find situations where one variable changes another's effect.
Visualise relationships — grouped scatter, partial-dependence, or line plots to spot non-parallel patterns.
Create a small candidate set — prioritise interactions supported by theory or evidence.
Preserve main effects — include the original variables with the interaction term.
Build inside a pipeline — avoid inconsistent preprocessing and leakage.
Compare fairly — identical cross-validation folds and metrics.
Regularise or select — L1/L2, tree importance, or permutation importance when many terms exist.
Interpret and document — record the formula, reason, units, reference levels, and validation impact.

content.text: When should you create one?

rows: Strong domain reason effects depend on each other
Linear model underfits a known combined effect
No theory, no visual pattern, tiny dataset
Feature uses info unavailable at prediction time

content.text: Mini practice activity
A company predicts monthly electricity consumption from temperature, household size, and whether the home uses air conditioning.

items: Create temperature × household_size. Explain what it may capture.
Create temperature × has_air_conditioning. Explain why AC homes may show a different temperature slope.
Fit a baseline linear model with main effects only.
Fit a second model with the two interactions.
Compare cross-validated MAE or RMSE.
Plot predicted consumption vs temperature separately for AC and non-AC homes.
Keep only interactions that improve validation performance and stay logically reasonable.

content.text: Temperature is likely to increase electricity use much more strongly in homes with air conditioning — producing non-parallel prediction lines for AC vs non-AC homes.
content.title: Expected insight

content.text: Quick revision

rows: A feature representing the combined effect of two or more variables.
The most common form: X1 × X2.
Non-parallel or crossing lines across groups.
Usually keep X1 and X2 when including X1 × X2.
The effect of one feature depends on the value of the other.
Especially important for linear and logistic regression.
Compare models using the same folds and metric.
Too many interactions increase dimensionality and overfitting.
Domain knowledge, centering/scaling, pipelines, and regularisation.

content.text: Key takeaways

items: Interaction features are used when variables do not act independently.
A product term lets the slope of one feature change with another feature.
Interactions can be numeric×numeric, numeric×categorical, or categorical×categorical.
Simple linear models need explicit interaction terms; tree models often learn them automatically.
Keep a feature only when it is meaningful, leakage-free, and improves validation performance.

content.text: In the electricity example, why should you keep temperature and household_size in the model even after adding temperature × household_size — and how would you decide the interaction is worth keeping?
content.title: Check your understanding

keyPoints: An interaction feature captures the combined effect of two or more variables — used when the effect of one feature depends on the value or category of another.
In a linear model, adding b3·(X1×X2) lets the slope of one feature change with the other; non-parallel or crossing group lines are the classic visual sign.
Interactions come in three forms — numeric×numeric, numeric×categorical (a slope per category), and categorical×categorical (joint categories); start with two-way terms.
Linear and logistic regression usually need explicit interaction terms; decision trees, random forests, and boosting often discover them automatically.
Keep main effects alongside the product term, center/scale to reduce multicollinearity, guard against leakage, and keep an interaction only if it improves validated performance.
commonMistakes: Dropping the main effects X1 and X2 when using X1×X2, making the interaction coefficient misleading.
Generating every possible pair of interactions, causing feature explosion and overfitting.
Interpreting a main-effect coefficient on its own when an interaction is present.
Building an interaction from information unavailable at prediction time (leakage) or trusting training accuracy instead of validation.

lessons.title: Polynomial Features
lessons.summary: How adding power and product columns (x², x³, x₁x₂) lets a model that is linear in its coefficients fit curved relationships. Covers the definition and one- and two-feature expansions, the types of polynomial terms and the meaning of degree, a study/sleep worked example, the feature-count formula C(n+d, d), how degree drives underfitting vs overfitting (with training/validation curves), the curved response surface for two inputs, a safe workflow with scaling and a scikit-learn Pipeline (PolynomialFeatures → StandardScaler → Ridge + cross-validation), degree selection, advantages/limitations including multicollinearity and the extrapolation warning, when polynomial features fit, common mistakes, a house-price mini example, and self-check.

content.text: Making a straight-line model bend

A linear model draws straight lines and flat planes — that is all it can do in its raw input space. Yet many real relationships curve: house value rises faster for larger homes, crop yield peaks and then falls with rainfall. Polynomial features are the trick that lets a model which is linear in its coefficients still fit these curves. Rather than change the algorithm, you change what you feed it: you add columns like x², x³, and x₁x₂.

content.caption: Figure 1. A degree-2 polynomial expansion of two inputs: [x₁, x₂] → [x₁, x₂, x₁², x₁x₂, x₂²]. The original row is expanded with power and interaction terms.

content.text: New numerical features created by raising existing features to powers and multiplying features together. They let a model that is linear in its coefficients represent curved or non-linear relationships in the original input space.
Polynomial feature engineering changes the input representation, not the learning algorithm. A linear model can then fit curves because it receives columns such as x², x³, or x₁x₂.
content.title: Core idea

content.text: These notes stay focused on polynomial features — what they are, how they are generated, how they influence model behaviour, and how to use them correctly. Related transformation and selection topics live in their own sub-modules.

One feature

content.title: Important connection

content.text: Types of polynomial terms

rows: Captures curvature within a single feature.
Captures a combined effect between features.
The intercept; often excluded to avoid duplication.

content.text: The degree is the maximum total exponent allowed in a generated term — higher degrees mean more flexible shapes:

rows: Degree-2 terms + x₁³, x₁²x₂, x₁x₂², x₂³
All products with total exponent ≤ degree

content.text: Worked numerical example

A dataset has two features: study hours (x₁) and sleep hours (x₂). A degree-2 transformation adds the power and interaction columns below (split into two tables so every column stays readable on a phone):
x₁² lets the effect of study time curve, while x₁x₂ lets the model learn that study hours may have a different effect at different sleep levels.
content.title: Interpretation

content.text: How many features are generated?
For n original features and maximum degree d, the number of polynomial columns (including the bias term) is a binomial coefficient:

content.expression:
Number of columns = C(n + d, d)
Excluding the bias term:  C(n + d, d) − 1
content.explanation: C(a, b) is the binomial coefficient ‘a choose b’.

content.text: The feature count grows combinatorially. A high degree with many original features can sharply increase memory use, training time, multicollinearity, and overfitting.
content.title: Why this matters

content.text: How degree changes model fit
The degree controls how much the model can bend. Too little and it misses the pattern; too much and it chases noise.

content.caption: Figure 2. The same non-linear data fitted by a degree-1 line (underfits), a degree-2 curve (captures the shape), and a degree-5 curve (starts wiggling toward the noise).

rows: Enough curvature for the main pattern
Many bends that follow small fluctuations

content.caption: Figure 3. As degree rises, training error keeps falling, but validation error falls, bottoms out in a balanced region, then rises again — the signature of overfitting.

content.text: Choose the degree using validation data or cross-validation — never by picking the degree that gives the smallest training error.
content.title: Model-selection rule

content.text: Multiple inputs: a curved surface
With two inputs, a quadratic expansion produces a curved response surface rather than a flat plane:

content.expression: ŷ = β₀ + β₁x₁ + β₂x₂ + β₃x₁² + β₄x₁x₂ + β₅x₂²

content.caption: Figure 4. Quadratic and interaction terms let a linear estimator predict a curved surface over two features x₁ and x₂.

items: β₃ and β₅ control curvature along each feature direction.
β₄ controls interaction: the effect of x₁ changes as x₂ changes.
The model can form curved boundaries or surfaces even though the estimator itself is linear.

content.text: Practical workflow

items: Start with a simple baseline using the original features.
Select only relevant numerical features for polynomial expansion.
Choose a small candidate degree, commonly 2 or 3.
Generate polynomial terms inside a preprocessing pipeline.
Scale the expanded features — powers can have very different magnitudes.
Train a regularised model such as Ridge or Lasso where appropriate.
Compare candidate degrees using cross-validation.
Evaluate once on a held-out test set and inspect residuals.

content.text: Why scaling matters

If x ranges from 0 to 100, then x² ranges up to 10,000 and x³ up to 1,000,000. These scale differences make optimisation unstable and distort regularisation penalties — so standardise after expansion.

Recommended order: polynomial expansion → standardisation → estimator. Put every step in one pipeline so the same transformations are learned from each training fold and applied consistently to validation/test data.
content.title: Pipeline order

content.text: scikit-learn example

content.code:
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures, StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

model = Pipeline([
    ("poly", PolynomialFeatures(degree=2, include_bias=False)),
    ("scale", StandardScaler()),
    ("regressor", Ridge(alpha=1.0)),
])

scores = cross_val_score(
    model, X, y, cv=5,
    scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error",
)

mean_rmse = -scores.mean()
model.fit(X, y)
content.explanation: Expansion, scaling, and a regularised estimator live in one pipeline, so cross-validation fits them only on each training fold — no leakage.

Columns such as x, x², and x³ are usually correlated, especially when x is not centred. This can make individual coefficients unstable even when predictions stay useful.

Categorical variables would be expanded blindly into powers.

Cross-validation shows no reliable gain over the baseline.

Select a small, meaningful numeric subset.
Complexity almost always improves training fit.

Assume house price depends on floor area x. A straight-line model assumes each extra square metre adds the same amount. A degree-2 feature x² lets the marginal effect change with size:

items: If β₂ > 0, price rises at an increasing rate as area grows.
If β₂ < 0, the model represents diminishing marginal value at larger sizes.
The sign and effect are interpreted over the observed area range, not in isolation.

Low degree, scaling, regularisation, pipelines, cross-validation.
