content.text: Answers

items: log1p(0) = 0, while ln(0) is undefined (−∞).
It does not remove outliers; it compresses their distances on the numerical scale.
Linear regression is affected by curvature, scale, and variance patterns, while a decision tree mainly uses ordering to choose splits.
Use expm1(z), which computes exp(z) − 1.
Compare original and transformed versions under the same validation procedure and keep whichever best supports performance, stability, and interpretation.

keyPoints: A log transformation replaces x with ln(x), log10(x), or log1p(x) — it compresses large values far more than small ones while keeping the original order.
Its main use is reducing strong right skew in positive features (income, price, counts) and turning multiplicative differences into additive ones.
Use ln/log10 for strictly positive data and log1p for non-negative data with zeros; ordinary logs are invalid for zero or negative values (use Yeo-Johnson/signed log instead).
Logs often help linear, distance-, and gradient-based models but rarely help tree models, which depend only on value ordering; always validate before/after.
When the target is logged, invert predictions (exp, 10^x, or expm1) and watch for retransformation bias when reporting the mean.
commonMistakes: Taking log(0) or the log of negative values instead of using log1p or a transform like Yeo-Johnson.
Log-transforming every numerical feature rather than only skewed/multiplicative ones with a validated reason.
Forgetting to inverse-transform a logged target (exp/expm1) before reporting predictions.
Comparing logged vs original features on different splits, or assuming tree models need logs.

lessons.title: Handling Skewed Distributions
lessons.summary: How to recognise and reshape skewed numerical features so they help rather than distort a model. Covers the definition and direction of skewness (named after the tail), why it matters (linearity, variance, distance/gradient models, outlier influence), detection via histograms/box plots/Q–Q plots and a skewness coefficient, a leakage-safe workflow, the main techniques — log/log1p, square-root and cube-root, Box-Cox, Yeo-Johnson, capping/winsorising, quantile transformation, binning and robust modelling — a comparison of what each handles and its trade-offs, a method-selection guide and decision flowchart, a monthly-spending worked example, NumPy and scikit-learn PowerTransformer pipeline code, model-family sensitivity, validation criteria, common mistakes, and self-check.

content.text: When one long tail distorts everything

A distribution is skewed when most observations bunch up in one region while a smaller number stretch out into a long tail on one side. Income, house prices, session durations — they all tend to have a few enormous values trailing far to the right. That asymmetry is not an error in itself, but it can quietly pull a model off course: distances get dominated by extremes, relationships bend, and optimisation becomes unstable. Handling skewness well is about deciding when, and how, to reshape such a feature.

content.caption: Figure 1. The direction of skewness is named after the longer tail: left-skew (tail points left), approximately symmetric (similar tails), and right-skew (tail points right).

content.text: The lack of symmetry in a numerical feature's distribution. A feature is skewed when most observations concentrate in one region while a smaller number form a long tail on one side.
The direction of skewness is named after the tail, not the side holding most observations. A right-skewed distribution has a long right tail; a left-skewed distribution has a long left tail.
content.title: Key idea

content.text: These notes focus on handling skewed numerical distributions as a feature-engineering task. They do not cover class or target imbalance, or general data cleaning except where it directly affects skewness.
content.title: Scope

content.text: What you'll be able to do

items: Define skewness and recognise positive, negative, and approximately symmetric distributions.
Detect skewness with histograms, box plots, summary statistics, and a skewness coefficient.
Select an appropriate transformation without causing data leakage.
Explain when log, square-root, Box-Cox, Yeo-Johnson, capping, or robust modelling fits.
Validate whether a transformation actually improves the pipeline.

rows: Adult height in a homogeneous group

content.text: Why skewness matters in ML
Skewness becomes a feature-engineering concern when it reduces model quality, destabilises optimisation, creates non-linear relationships, or lets a few extreme values dominate learning.

items: Linear relationships — a transform can make the feature–target relationship closer to linear.
Variance stability — skewed values often spread more as they grow; transforms reduce this heteroscedasticity.
Distance-based models — KNN, K-means, and clustering can be dominated by large values.
Gradient-based optimisation — extreme scales make training less stable, especially with poor scaling.
Interpretability — residual plots and coefficients can be easier to read after a justified transform.
Outlier influence — a long tail often holds high-leverage points (though skewness ≠ outliers).

content.text: Skewness describes the overall shape; outliers are individual unusual observations. A feature can be skewed with no obvious outliers, and can contain outliers while staying roughly symmetric.
content.title: Important distinction

content.text: How to detect skewness
Visual inspection

content.caption: Figure 2. A strongly right-skewed feature: many smaller observations and a long tail of large values, with the mean (31.8) pulled above the median (20.2).

items: Histogram — reveals concentration, gaps, multiple peaks, and tail direction.
Density plot — a smoothed view of the distribution shape.
Box plot — highlights median, spread, and points beyond the whiskers.
Q–Q plot — assesses how strongly the distribution departs from normality.

content.text: Summary statistics

rows: Right skew pulls mean above median; left skew below.
A big jump in upper percentiles suggests a long right tail.
Sign gives direction, magnitude gives strength — not used alone.
Invalid values create artificial skew; fix before transforming.

content.text: Interpreting a skewness coefficient
A common rule of thumb — descriptive guidelines, not universal laws. Sample size, model type, and business meaning matter too.

rows: Usually keep as-is unless diagnostics show a problem.
Inspect visuals; validate a transform if the model may benefit.
Investigate domain causes, outliers, and suitable transforms.

content.text: A correct workflow

items: Understand what the feature represents and whether the tail is realistic.
Correct invalid values and investigate extreme observations before transforming.
Split the data into training and validation/test sets.
Fit any learned transformer using the training data only.
Transform the validation/test data with the already-fitted transformer.
Compare cross-validation performance, residuals, stability, and interpretability.
Keep the transformation only if it provides a meaningful benefit.

content.text: Box-Cox parameters, Yeo-Johnson parameters, quantile mappings, capping thresholds, and similar statistics must be learned from training data. Learning them from the full dataset leaks validation/test information.
content.title: Data-leakage warning

content.text: The main techniques
Log transformation

content.expression: x' = log(x)   or, when zeros are present,   x' = log(1 + x)

items: Best for non-negative, strongly right-skewed features.
Compresses large values more than small ones.
Useful for income, prices, counts, durations, transaction amounts.
Never apply ordinary log to zero/negative values — use log1p for zeros, Yeo-Johnson for negatives.

content.caption: Figure 3. The same feature after log1p: the long right tail is compressed and the mean and median coincide (both ≈ 3.05).

content.text: Square-root and cube-root
Gentler than log — shown split into two tables so every column stays readable on a phone:

rows: Moderate skew when sign should be preserved

content.text: Box-Cox
Box-Cox searches for a power parameter λ that makes a strictly positive feature more Gaussian-like or variance-stable. The parameter is learned from the training data.

items: Requires every value strictly greater than zero.
A flexible family; λ ≈ 0 behaves like a log transform.
Useful when a fixed transform (log, sqrt) is not clearly justified.

content.text: Yeo-Johnson
Similar to Box-Cox but handles zero and negative values — often the safest learned power transform when a feature crosses zero.
Capping / winsorising
Capping replaces values beyond chosen thresholds with the threshold value. It is mainly outlier control, not a complete cure for skewness.

items: Use when extremes are measurement errors, operational anomalies, or implausible.
Common thresholds: domain limits or training-set percentiles (1st and 99th).
Avoid capping valid rare observations — they may carry important signal.

content.text: Quantile transformation
QuantileTransformer maps ranks to a target distribution (uniform or normal). It can strongly reduce skewness but changes distances and can hurt interpretability.

A quantile transform can produce an attractive distribution while distorting the original spacing between values. Validate carefully for distance-based models and when numeric differences must stay interpretable.
content.title: Use with caution

content.text: Binning and robust modelling

items: Binning — converts a continuous feature into intervals; reduces tail sensitivity but loses numeric detail.
Robust scaling — uses median and IQR; reduces extreme-scale influence but does not remove skewness.
Tree-based models — usually insensitive to monotonic transforms; transform only if validation shows a benefit.
Generalised linear models — sometimes change the target distribution/link function instead of transforming every skewed predictor.

content.text: Comparing the choices
Different transforms reduce skewness by different amounts. The two tables below split a full comparison so it stays mobile-friendly — first what each method can handle, then its trade-offs:

rows: Strong compression of a right tail
Safe for non-negative data with zeros
May be too weak for severe skew
Must be fitted inside the pipeline

content.caption: Figure 4. Skewness on the example dataset falls from 4.32 (original) to 1.65 (square root), 0.16 (log1p), and 0.00 (Yeo-Johnson).

content.text: Method-selection guide

rows: Compresses large values and stabilises spread.
Both support zero; log1p is stronger.
Preserve all observations without manual shifting.
May be a data-quality issue, not the distribution.
Trees often need no distributional correction.
Coefficients must stay in original units
Transforms change the meaning of a one-unit change.

content.caption: Figure 5. Decision guide: only transform if skew is meaningful and harms validation; then choose by value range (positive → log1p/sqrt/Box-Cox, mixed signs → Yeo-Johnson, dominant outliers → capping) and always fit on training data before validating.

content.text: Worked example: monthly spending
Monthly spending: 25, 28, 30, 32, 35, 38, 42, 50, 75, 200. Most customers spend 25–75, but one spends 200 — strongly right-skewed, with mean 55.5 and median 36.5. Applying log1p:

items: The large value 200 is compressed much more than the smaller values.
Customer order is preserved — log1p is monotonic.
The transformed coefficient is on a log scale, so interpretation must be explained.
The transform reduces skewness but may not remove it fully; validation decides if it helps.

content.text: Python implementation
Inspecting skewness

content.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

feature = df["monthly_spending"]
print("Skewness:", feature.skew())
print(feature.describe(percentiles=[0.50, 0.75, 0.90, 0.95, 0.99]))

feature.hist(bins=30)
plt.xlabel("Monthly spending")
plt.ylabel("Frequency")
plt.show()
content.explanation: skew() gives the coefficient; the percentiles and histogram confirm the shape and tail.

content.text: Simple log1p transform

content.code:
import numpy as np

df["monthly_spending_log"] = np.log1p(df["monthly_spending"])
print(df["monthly_spending_log"].skew())
content.explanation: Re-checking skew() after the transform confirms whether it moved toward symmetry.

content.text: Leakage-safe transform inside a pipeline

content.code:
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import PowerTransformer, StandardScaler
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

skewed_features = ["income", "monthly_spending", "session_duration"]

skew_pipeline = Pipeline(steps=[
    ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
    ("power", PowerTransformer(method="yeo-johnson", standardize=False)),
    ("scaler", StandardScaler()),
])

preprocessor = ColumnTransformer(
    transformers=[("skewed", skew_pipeline, skewed_features)],
    remainder="passthrough",
)

model = Pipeline(steps=[
    ("preprocess", preprocessor),
    ("regressor", LinearRegression()),
])

model.fit(X_train, y_train)
predictions = model.predict(X_test)
content.explanation: During cross-validation, the Yeo-Johnson parameter is learned separately inside each training fold and applied to the validation fold — which prevents leakage.

content.text: Model sensitivity to skew

rows: Compare versions; examine coefficients and diagnostics.
Large values dominate distance; transform and scale when justified.
Scale matters; skew can affect geometry and margins.
Transforming heavy tails can aid optimisation; scaling essential.
Monotonic transforms give similar split orderings.
Often fine untransformed, but extreme tails can affect behaviour.

content.text: A distribution does not need to look perfectly normal. The goal is better generalisation, stability, and interpretability for the chosen model — not a cosmetically ideal histogram.
content.title: Success criterion

content.text: How to validate a transformation

items: Compare cross-validation metrics using the original and transformed feature.
Check residual plots for reduced patterns or changing variance (linear models).
Check whether train–validation performance becomes more stable across folds.
Confirm the transformed values stay meaningful and create no infinities or missing values.
Evaluate performance on relevant subgroups, especially tail observations.
Keep both original and transformed versions only when multicollinearity and overfitting are controlled.
Document the exact transformation and its inverse for reporting.

content.text: Common mistakes and corrections

rows: Many models don't need symmetric predictors.
log1p for non-negatives; Yeo-Johnson for mixed signs.
Use a principled transform and record the rule.
Fit the transformer before the split
Leaks distribution info from the test set.
Fit inside a pipeline on training data only.
Inspect the full shape; investigate extremes separately.
Judge success by reduced skew only
A lower statistic may not improve prediction.
State the scale and back-transform where appropriate.

content.text: Quick revision

items: Definition — skewness is asymmetry caused by a longer tail on one side.
Positive skew — long right tail; mean often greater than median.
Negative skew — long left tail; mean often less than median.
Detection — histograms, box plots, percentiles, mean–median comparison, skewness coefficient.
Main methods — log1p, square root, cube root, Box-Cox, Yeo-Johnson, capping, quantile, binning, robust modelling.
Leakage rule — learn transformation parameters using training data only.
Final decision — keep a transform only when it improves validated behaviour or interpretability.

content.text: Handle skewness as a model-dependent engineering decision: understand the feature, select a mathematically valid method, fit it without leakage, and retain it only after validation.
content.title: One-sentence takeaway

content.text: Self-check

1. Why is a right-skewed distribution named after the right tail rather than where most observations sit? 2. Which transformation suits a feature that contains negative values and zero? 3. Why can a lower skewness coefficient still fail to improve model performance? 4. What data leakage occurs when a PowerTransformer is fitted on the full dataset? 5. Why might a random forest need no transformation even when a feature is strongly skewed?
content.title: Test yourself

content.text: Answers

items: Because skewness direction is defined by the longer tail; most observations sit at the opposite, compact end.
Yeo-Johnson (or cube root) — both handle zero and negative values without a manual shift.
A more symmetric shape does not guarantee better prediction; the model may not benefit, so validation must confirm it.
The transform's parameters are learned using validation/test observations too, leaking their information into training and inflating performance.
Trees split on value ordering, which monotonic transforms preserve — so the splits (and results) are essentially unchanged.

keyPoints: Skewness is asymmetry from a longer tail on one side (named after the tail); it matters when it harms linearity, variance, distance/gradient models, or lets extremes dominate.
Detect it with histograms, box plots, Q–Q plots, mean-vs-median comparison, and a skewness coefficient (|s|>1 is strongly skewed) — never the statistic alone.

Main techniques: log/log1p and sqrt/cube-root (fixed), Box-Cox (positive only) and Yeo-Johnson (handles zero/negatives) as learned power transforms, plus capping, quantile transform, binning, and robust modelling.
Learned transformers (Box-Cox/Yeo-Johnson params, quantile maps, capping thresholds) must be fitted on training data only, inside a pipeline, to avoid leakage.
Keep a transformation only when validation shows real benefit — tree models are usually insensitive, and reduced skewness alone does not guarantee better prediction.
commonMistakes: Automatically transforming every skewed feature instead of using diagnostics and cross-validation.
Applying ordinary log to zero or negative values rather than log1p or Yeo-Johnson.
Fitting a PowerTransformer/quantile transform on the full dataset before splitting (data leakage).
Confusing skewness with outliers, or judging success by reduced skewness rather than validated performance.

lessons.title: Date and Time Features
lessons.summary: How to turn raw timestamps into meaningful, leakage-free model inputs. Covers why models need engineered time features, the main types (calendar and clock components, boolean indicators, elapsed time, cyclical encodings, lag and rolling features, temporal interactions), extracting date parts with pandas, reading daily/weekly patterns from plots, meaningful time bands, cyclical sine/cosine encoding for circular variables, elapsed-time/age/tenure/recency features, lag and rolling-window features with a shift to avoid leakage, temporal interaction features, a delivery-time worked example, data-quality issues (formats, timezones, DST, ordering), chronological validation, per-model encoding choices, a practical checklist, and a practice activity.

content.text: Teaching a model to read the calendar

A timestamp like 2026-08-04 14:35 means a great deal to a person — a Tuesday afternoon in late summer — but almost nothing to a model, which sees only an opaque number or string. Date and time features unlock that hidden meaning, turning one raw timestamp into signals a model can learn from: the hour, the weekday, whether it is a weekend, how long a customer has been active, and what happened in the recent past. Done carefully, they capture rush hours, weekly rhythms, seasons, and recency; done carelessly, they leak the future into the past.

content.caption: Figure 1. From a raw timestamp to model-ready features: raw timestamp → parse to a datetime type → extract features (hour, day, month, lag) → numeric model input.

content.text: Numerical or categorical variables created from timestamps, calendar dates, durations, or ordered historical observations. They help a model learn patterns related to hours, days, weeks, seasons, recency, elapsed time, and previous values.

A raw date such as “2026-08-04 14:35” is rarely useful by itself. It becomes useful after extraction into features such as hour = 14, weekday = Tuesday, month = August, weekend = 0, or time_since_signup = 92 days.
content.title: Core idea

content.text: These notes stay focused on creating, transforming, validating, and using date and time features in ML datasets.
content.title: Scope

content.text: Why models need engineered time features

items: Most ML algorithms need numeric inputs and do not understand calendar meaning automatically.
Time often holds repeating patterns — rush hours, weekends, month-end effects, seasonal demand.
Recent history can predict the future, so lag and rolling-window features matter in time-dependent data.
Elapsed time often represents ageing, recency, waiting time, tenure, machine usage, or time to failure.

rows: An event on a Tuesday afternoon

content.text: The main types of time feature
Extracting calendar and clock parts
Take event_time = 2026-08-04 14:35:20. A rich set of components can be pulled straight out of it:

content.code:
import pandas as pd

df['event_time'] = pd.to_datetime(df['event_time'], errors='coerce')
df['year'] = df['event_time'].dt.year
df['month'] = df['event_time'].dt.month
df['weekday'] = df['event_time'].dt.dayofweek        # Monday=0
df['hour'] = df['event_time'].dt.hour
df['is_weekend'] = (df['weekday'] >= 5).astype(int)
df['is_month_end'] = df['event_time'].dt.is_month_end.astype(int)
content.explanation: errors='coerce' turns invalid strings into NaT so bad dates surface as missing values instead of wrong features.

content.text: Always parse the timestamp first. Invalid date strings should become missing values (NaT) and be handled explicitly, not silently produce incorrect features.
content.title: Parse before extracting

content.text: Look before you model
Plotting a candidate time feature against the target reveals whether it is likely to carry predictive information at all.

content.caption: Figure 2. Hour-of-day traffic reveals operational peaks and quiet periods — a clear evening peak around 17:00 and a night-time low.
Figure 3. Orders by day of week show weekly demand differences — weekends run noticeably higher than mid-week.

content.text: Activity is not constant across time. A model given hour and weekday information can represent these systematic changes.
content.title: Interpretation

content.text: Meaningful time categories
Sometimes a broad band is easier to interpret than an exact clock value — an hour can be grouped into a period of the day:
Grouping reduces detail. It can improve simplicity and interpretability, but exact hour or cyclical encoding may perform better when patterns change gradually.
content.title: Use carefully

content.text: Cyclical encoding

Hours, weekdays, and months are circular: 23:00 is right next to 00:00, yet plain integer encoding treats them as 23 apart. Cyclical encoding fixes this by mapping each value onto a circle with a sine and a cosine component.

content.caption: Figure 4. Circular encoding places each hour on a circle, so 23:00 and 00:00 sit close together — preserving the natural closeness of a cycle's end and start.

content.code:
import numpy as np

df['hour_sin'] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * df['hour'] / 24)
df['hour_cos'] = np.cos(2 * np.pi * df['hour'] / 24)

df['month_sin'] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * (df['month'] - 1) / 12)
df['month_cos'] = np.cos(2 * np.pi * (df['month'] - 1) / 12)
content.explanation: Each cyclical variable needs BOTH sin and cos — together they give every value a unique, circular position.

content.text: Elapsed time: age, tenure, recency
Elapsed-time features measure the distance between two dates. They usually carry a direct real-world meaning and often beat the raw dates.

rows: How long the customer has been active

content.code:
reference_date = pd.Timestamp('2026-08-04')

df['tenure_days'] = (reference_date - df['signup_date']).dt.days
df['days_since_purchase'] = (reference_date - df['last_purchase']).dt.days
df['delivery_hours'] = (
    df['delivery_time'] - df['order_time']
).dt.total_seconds() / 3600

content.text: The reference date must be the prediction date or earlier. Do not compute “days until cancellation” or use future timestamps that would be unavailable when the prediction is made.
content.title: No-leakage rule

content.text: Lag and rolling-window features
For ordered observations, the recent past becomes a set of predictors — core to forecasting, demand prediction, sensor monitoring, finance, and user-activity modelling.

rows: Sales the same weekday last week

content.caption: Figure 5. A 3-day rolling mean (orange) smooths the short-term noise in daily sales (blue) and summarizes the recent level.

content.code:
df = df.sort_values('date')

df['sales_lag_1'] = df['sales'].shift(1)
df['sales_lag_7'] = df['sales'].shift(7)
df['sales_roll_mean_7'] = df['sales'].shift(1).rolling(7).mean()
df['sales_roll_std_7'] = df['sales'].shift(1).rolling(7).std()
content.explanation: The shift(1) before rolling() guarantees each window uses only PAST data — without it, the current value leaks in.

content.text: Compute lag and rolling features only after sorting by time. In grouped data, create them separately within each customer, store, machine, or other entity.
content.title: Critical detail

content.text: Temporal interaction features
A time feature can behave differently in another context. Interaction features capture these combined effects — Monday 08:00 is a very different situation from Saturday 08:00.

rows: Seasonality may vary across product types
Holiday impact may differ by location
Rain may affect demand differently at commute times
Ageing behaviour may differ by plan

content.caption: Figure 6. A day-of-week × hour heatmap exposes patterns hidden by either feature alone — e.g. a strong weekend-afternoon activity block.

content.text: Worked example: delivery-time prediction
The target is delivery duration in minutes. The raw dataset has order_time, dispatch_time, customer location, traffic level, and actual delivery_time. From these we can engineer:
The original timestamp becomes interpretable numeric signals. The model can now learn that deliveries placed during evening peaks, weekends, or high local demand may take longer.
content.title: Model-ready result

content.text: Data-quality and preprocessing issues

rows: Specify format and locale when parsing
Investigate; impute only if justified, or add a flag
Can distort counts or rolling stats
Check entity keys and event identifiers
Same instant at different local times
Convert to a common timezone, then derive locals
Resample or use actual elapsed time
Use only data available at prediction time

content.text: Timezone example

content.code:
# Parse in UTC, then convert for local calendar features
df['event_time_utc'] = pd.to_datetime(df['event_time'], utc=True)
df['event_time_local'] = df['event_time_utc'].dt.tz_convert('Asia/Karachi')
df['local_hour'] = df['event_time_local'].dt.hour

content.text: Store event time in UTC for consistency. Derive local-hour or local-weekday features only when local behaviour is relevant to the prediction problem.
content.title: Best practice

content.text: Correct validation for time data
A random train–test split can let future observations influence training. For time-dependent problems, split chronologically — train on the past, test on the future.

rows: Estimate performance on future unseen data

content.text: Fit preprocessing steps, encoders, rolling statistics, and feature-selection decisions using training data only. The test period must stay untouched until final evaluation.
content.title: Rule

content.text: Choosing encodings per model

rows: Raw hour integers imply a false straight-line effect
Split on thresholds; may still gain from cyclical
Usually strong for structured temporal data
Good for complex sequences and high volume
Validation and leakage control are essential

content.text: Do not automatically create every possible feature. A smaller set of meaningful, leakage-free features usually beats many noisy date parts.
content.title: Keep it lean

content.text: Practical checklist

items: Parse the date/timestamp into a proper datetime type.
Confirm the timezone, date format, and meaning of each timestamp.
Sort records by entity and time before creating historical features.
Extract only components that could logically influence the target.
Use cyclical encoding for repeating variables when circular distance matters.
Create elapsed-time features using a valid prediction-time reference date.
Shift rolling windows so they contain past values only.
Use chronological validation for time-dependent observations.
Inspect plots to confirm temporal patterns actually exist.
Remove redundant or unstable time features after validation.

content.text: Quick summary

rows: Break a date into useful parts
Train on past, test on future

content.text: Mini practice activity
A dataset has customer_id, purchase_time, amount, signup_date, and last_purchase_time. Create these features:

items: purchase_hour and purchase_weekday
is_weekend
hour_sin and hour_cos
customer_tenure_days at purchase time
days_since_previous_purchase
customer rolling mean of the previous five purchase amounts

content.text: All historical features must be calculated separately for each customer and use only purchases that occurred before the current row — otherwise you leak the future.
content.title: Check your logic

content.text: Why must the rolling mean of the previous five purchases be computed within each customer and with a shift, rather than across the whole sorted dataset?
content.title: Think it through

content.text: Answer

Mixing customers would average one person's history into another's, and without a shift the current purchase would be included in its own “past” — both corrupt the feature. Grouping by customer_id and shifting by one keeps each value based only on that customer's earlier purchases, which is exactly the information available at prediction time.

keyPoints: Raw timestamps must be parsed to a datetime type, then decomposed into numeric signals — calendar/clock parts, boolean indicators, and durations — because models don't understand calendars.
Cyclical variables (hour, weekday, month) need sine/cosine encoding so the end and start of a cycle stay close (23:00 near 00:00).
Elapsed-time features (tenure, recency, duration) must use a reference date at or before prediction time — never a future timestamp.
Lag and rolling features must be sorted by time, computed within each entity, and shifted so each window uses only past values.
Time-dependent data requires chronological (past→future) splits and training-only fitting, and each model family prefers different encodings.
commonMistakes: Extracting features from unparsed strings, or letting invalid dates silently produce wrong features instead of NaT.
Integer-encoding cyclical variables (so 23:00 and 00:00 look far apart) instead of using sine/cosine.
Building lag/rolling features without sorting by time, without grouping by entity, or without a shift — leaking the current or future value.
Using a random train-test split (or a future reference date) for time-dependent data, causing leakage and over-optimistic results.

lessons.title: Text-based Features
lessons.summary: How to convert written language into numeric inputs a model can use. Covers why text needs feature engineering, task-aware preprocessing (tokenization, stemming, lemmatization, keeping negation/emojis), and the main feature families — structural/statistical features, Bag-of-Words, binary presence, n-grams, TF-IDF (with the TF×IDF formula), keyword/lexicon and sentiment/readability features, and dense embeddings. Includes a reviews-into-features worked example, a comparison of methods, sparse vs dense matrices, a scikit-learn TfidfVectorizer example with unigrams and bigrams, dimensionality control, common problems (high dimensionality, OOV words, negation, leakage), a best-practice checklist, quick revision, and a spam/phishing practice activity.

content.text: Turning words into numbers

A machine-learning model cannot read a sentence. It sees only numbers — so before text can predict anything, it has to be converted into a fixed set of numeric inputs. That conversion is text feature engineering: extracting measurable signals from written language, from something as simple as “how many words?” to a rich TF-IDF matrix or a dense meaning-carrying embedding. The right representation depends entirely on the task.

content.caption: Figure 1. The text feature-engineering pipeline: raw text → clean → tokenize → vectorize → ML model.

content.text: Numerical or categorical variables extracted from written language so that a machine-learning algorithm can process it. Raw text contains words, symbols, and structure, but most models expect a fixed set of numeric inputs.
A sentence is not used directly. It is transformed into values such as word counts, TF-IDF weights, sentence length, a sentiment score, or an embedding vector.
content.title: Simple idea

content.text: These notes stay focused on feature engineering for text data. Model-training details appear only where they help explain how text features are used.
content.title: Scope

content.text: What you'll be able to do

items: Define text-based features and explain why text must become numbers.
Create structural, count-based, TF-IDF, n-gram, keyword, and embedding features.
Compare common text representations and pick a suitable method for a task.
Recognise practical problems — sparse matrices, high dimensionality, and data leakage.

content.text: Why raw text needs feature engineering

items: Most traditional models cannot compute directly with words.
Documents have different lengths, but models generally need fixed-length input vectors.
The same meaning appears in different forms — “run”, “running”, “ran”.
Some words are common but uninformative; others are rare but highly meaningful.
Word order can change meaning — “not good” versus “good”.

rows: Question mark = 1; question pattern; topic = return/refund

content.text: Basic text preparation
Preprocessing and feature engineering are connected. Cleaning should preserve the information that matters for the prediction task — not strip it away.

rows: Treats capital and lowercase as one token
Reduces noise when punctuation isn't useful
Splits text into words or subwords
Cuts words to a rough root
Maps words to a dictionary base form

content.text: Do not remove punctuation, negation words, or emojis automatically. They can be valuable in sentiment, fraud, toxicity, and intent-detection tasks.
content.title: Important

content.text: The main types of text feature
Structural and statistical features
These describe the shape of the text rather than its exact vocabulary.

content.caption: Figure 2. Two simple numeric features — review length and exclamation-mark count — already spread documents apart before any vocabulary is used.

content.text: Bag-of-Words (BoW)
Bag-of-Words builds a vocabulary and records how often each vocabulary word appears in a document. It ignores grammar and usually word order.
Vocabulary [machine, learning, makes, useful, predictions]. The sentence “machine learning makes useful predictions” becomes [1, 1, 1, 1, 1].
content.title: Example vocabulary

content.caption: Figure 3. Bag-of-Words counts each vocabulary token's frequency in one sentence.

items: Strength — simple, fast, and easy to interpret.
Limitation — produces many zeros and understands neither meaning nor order.

content.text: Binary word-presence features
A binary representation records whether a word appears, not how many times — useful when repeated occurrences should not dominate the value.

content.caption: Figure 4. A binary presence vector for a short review: 1 where a vocabulary word occurs (product, fast, delivery, amazing), 0 otherwise (bad, slow).

content.text: N-gram features
N-grams are sequences of n consecutive tokens — unigrams (one), bigrams (two), trigrams (three). They capture limited word order and short phrases.

content.caption: Figure 5. Unigrams (not, very, good) versus bigrams (not very, very good) over the phrase “not very good”.

content.text: A unigram model sees “good”, but a bigram or trigram can preserve the negative phrase “not good” or “not very good”.
content.title: Why n-grams matter

content.text: TF-IDF features
TF-IDF (Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency) gives higher weight to terms frequent in one document but not frequent across every document.

content.explanation: TF measures how often a term occurs in the current document; IDF reduces the weight of words common across many documents.

items: TF measures how often a term occurs in the current document.
IDF reduces the importance of words that occur in many documents.
The result highlights words that better distinguish one document from others.

content.caption: Figure 6. An illustrative TF-IDF matrix across three documents: a zero means the term is absent; a larger value means the term is more distinctive for that document.

content.text: Keyword, pattern, and lexicon features
Domain knowledge can be turned into targeted, highly interpretable features that supplement BoW or TF-IDF.
A lexicon may score “good” as positive, but it can fail on sarcasm, negation, and domain-specific meanings.
content.title: Use carefully

content.text: Sentiment and readability features

items: Sentiment polarity — a score for negative, neutral, or positive language.
Subjectivity — opinion-based versus factual wording.
Readability score — how easy the text is to read.
Lexical diversity — the proportion of unique words.
Average sentence length — a simple indicator of writing complexity.

content.text: Word and sentence embeddings
Embeddings represent words, sentences, or documents as dense numeric vectors, placing similar meanings close together in vector space. Unlike BoW, they capture semantic relationships.
Worked example: reviews into features

Take three reviews — R1 “Excellent product and fast delivery!”, R2 “Product is good but delivery is slow.”, and R3 “Bad quality. I want a refund.” The tables below split their engineered features so every column stays readable on a phone:
A step-by-step transformation:

items: Clean and tokenize each review while preserving useful punctuation or negation.
Create structural features such as word count and punctuation count.
Create domain flags such as contains “refund”, “slow”, or “bad”.
Create a BoW or TF-IDF matrix for vocabulary-based information.
Optionally add a sentiment score or an embedding vector.
Combine the selected features into one final input matrix for the model.

content.text: Comparing common methods
Each representation captures something different — split into two tables (what it captures and its strengths, then its limits and best starting use) to stay mobile-friendly:
Sparse and dense matrices

Bag-of-Words and TF-IDF are usually sparse — each document uses only a small portion of the full vocabulary, so most values are zero. Embeddings are usually dense and much lower-dimensional. Consider a tiny BoW matrix (split so every term column stays readable):
The matrix is mostly zeros. With thousands of vocabulary terms, memory-efficient sparse-matrix storage becomes important.
content.title: Observation

content.text: BoW and TF-IDF usually create one dimension per vocabulary term. Embeddings use a smaller dense vector in which each dimension is learned and not directly named.
content.title: Key distinction

content.text: Python example: TF-IDF with n-grams

content.code:
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer

texts = [
    "excellent product and fast delivery",
    "delivery was slow",
    "bad product request refund",
]

vectorizer = TfidfVectorizer(
    lowercase=True,
    ngram_range=(1, 2),   # unigrams and bigrams
    min_df=1,
)

X = vectorizer.fit_transform(texts)
print(vectorizer.get_feature_names_out())
print(X.toarray())
content.explanation: Each row is a document, each column a unigram or bigram feature, and the values are TF-IDF weights. Fit the vectorizer on training data only.

content.text: Controlling dimensionality

items: Set a maximum vocabulary size to keep only the most useful terms.
Use min_df to remove extremely rare terms that may be noise.
Use max_df to remove terms appearing in nearly all documents.
Choose an n-gram range carefully — larger n-grams greatly increase dimensions.
Apply chi-square, mutual information, or model-based selection when appropriate.
Use dimensionality reduction only when it supports the model and preserves useful information.

content.text: Common problems and solutions

rows: Each document has few vocabulary items
Use sparse formats and suitable linear models
Use subword features, hashing, or embeddings
Fit preprocessing on training data only
Add domain lexicons or domain-specific reps

content.text: Best-practice checklist

items: Start with a simple baseline — TF-IDF plus a linear classifier.
Preserve text signals that matter — negation, punctuation, emojis.
Fit the vocabulary and all learned transformations on training data only.
Compare word-level and character-level features when spelling varies.
Inspect the most important features to detect bias, leakage, and shortcuts.
Evaluate more than accuracy when classes are imbalanced.
Use embeddings when semantic similarity matters, but keep interpretability where required.

content.text: Quick revision

rows: A measurable value extracted from written language
A text unit — word, subword, or character
The set of terms known to the vectorizer
Counts vocabulary terms in each document
A sequence of n consecutive tokens
Weights terms by local frequency and global rarity
A dense learned vector representing meaning
Using val/test information while building features

content.text: Text feature engineering converts language into structured numbers. Structural features aid interpretability; BoW and TF-IDF give strong baselines; n-grams preserve short phrases; embeddings capture meaning. The best representation depends on the task, dataset size, model, interpretability needs, and compute.
content.title: Key takeaway

content.text: Mini practice activity
For the message below, identify at least eight possible text features:
“URGENT! Your payment failed. Click https://example.com now.”
content.title: Message

items: Suggested features: word count, character count, uppercase ratio, exclamation count, URL count, contains “urgent”, contains “payment”, contains “failed”, imperative-word flag, and a sentiment/urgency score.
Then represent the same message using BoW or TF-IDF and compare it with the manually designed features.

content.text: Which of the features above would most strongly flag this message as spam or phishing, and why is combining structural flags with TF-IDF often better than either alone?
content.title: Think it through

content.text: Answer

The URL count, the all-caps “URGENT” (high uppercase ratio), the exclamation mark, and the urgency/payment keywords are the strongest phishing signals. Structural flags capture format and intent cues that TF-IDF misses, while TF-IDF captures distinctive vocabulary the flags don't enumerate — so together they give the classifier both the shape and the content of the message.

keyPoints: Text must be converted into fixed-length numeric vectors; text features range from simple structural counts to Bag-of-Words, TF-IDF, n-grams, and dense embeddings.
Preprocessing (lowercasing, tokenization, stemming/lemmatization) should preserve task-critical signals like negation, punctuation, and emojis rather than strip them.
TF-IDF weights terms by local frequency and global rarity to highlight distinctive words; n-grams preserve short phrases like “not good” that unigrams lose.
BoW/TF-IDF are sparse and high-dimensional (one dimension per term); embeddings are dense, low-dimensional, and capture semantic similarity.
Fit the vocabulary and all learned transformations on training data only, and control dimensionality with max vocabulary size, min_df/max_df, and feature selection.
commonMistakes: Automatically stripping punctuation, negation, or emojis that carry meaning for the task.
Fitting the vectorizer on the full dataset (including validation/test), leaking information.
Relying on unigrams alone so negated phrases like “not good” look like “good”.
Letting vocabulary and n-grams explode dimensionality instead of tuning min_df/max_df or selecting features.

lessons.title: Aggregated Features
lessons.summary: How to summarize many related records into one meaningful value per entity or time window. Covers the definition and components of an aggregated feature, why aggregation matters (event→model-ready data, behaviour patterns, noise reduction, predictive power, data-size control), common operations (count, sum, mean, median, min, max, std, unique count, ratio, recency), the creation steps, a customer-purchase worked example, time-based windows (daily/weekly/monthly/rolling/expanding/recent), aggregation by data type, pandas groupby and rolling code, derived aggregates, design decisions, the data-leakage risk with a cutoff-date rule, common mistakes, a best-practice checklist, and a driver-lateness practice activity.

content.text: Summarizing many rows into one

Most datasets record events — one row per order, per click, per sensor reading. But a model usually needs one row per thing it is predicting: one customer, one product, one machine. Aggregated features bridge that gap. They roll many detailed records up into compact summaries — total spend, average order value, purchases in the last 30 days — that describe behaviour over time far better than any single event or raw ID.

content.caption: Figure 1. Grouping transaction-level rows by customer turns many order records into one aggregated row per customer (orders, total, average).

content.text: New variables created by summarizing several related records into one meaningful value. The records are usually grouped by an entity (customer, product, patient, machine) or by a time window (day, week, month).

content.expression: Aggregated feature = Group records + Apply a summary operation
content.explanation: First decide what to group by, then choose the operation (count, sum, mean, …) that summarizes each group.

content.text: Many rows become a smaller number of summary values. Ten purchase records can become total spending, average order value, and number of purchases for one customer.
content.title: Simple idea

content.text: These notes focus only on aggregated features. General data cleaning, model training, and unrelated preprocessing are covered elsewhere.
content.title: Scope

content.text: What you'll be able to do

items: Define aggregated features in simple terms.
Understand why aggregation is useful in ML datasets.
Apply count, sum, mean, minimum, maximum, and standard deviation.
Create entity-level and time-window features using grouped data.
Recognise data leakage, incorrect grouping, and other common mistakes.

rows: The entity or window being summarized
The detailed rows inside the group
The resulting value used by the model

content.text: Why aggregated features matter

items: Convert event data into model-ready data — many event rows become one row per prediction unit.
Reveal behaviour patterns — totals, averages, frequency, and recency describe long-term behaviour, not a single event.
Reduce noise — means, medians, and rolling summaries smooth random fluctuations.
Improve predictive power — purchase frequency or days-since-last-order beats a raw ID.
Control data size — millions of event rows shrink to a manageable entity-level table.

content.text: Common aggregation operations

The choice of operation depends on the problem — a count describes frequency, a sum describes volume, a mean describes typical size, and a standard deviation describes stability. The two tables below split a full reference so every column stays readable on a phone:
How aggregated features are created

items: Choose the prediction unit — e.g. one customer per row.
Identify the detailed records linked to that unit — e.g. all of the customer's orders.
Select suitable aggregation operations — count, sum, mean.
Calculate the new values for every group.
Join the aggregated table back to the modelling dataset.

content.text: Worked example: customer purchases
An online shop stores one row per order:
Step by step for customer C01:
Repeating this for every customer gives a model-ready, one-row-per-customer table (split into two tables sharing the Customer key to stay mobile-friendly):

content.caption: Figure 2. Total spend per customer — a single aggregated feature that lets the model compare customers directly.

content.text: The model can now compare customers directly. C01 spends the most of the three worked-example customers, while C03 has the lowest average order value.
content.title: Interpretation

content.text: Time-based aggregated features
Aggregations can be computed within fixed or moving time windows, helping the model see both recent and long-term behaviour.

rows: Moving window that updates over time
All data from start to now
Events in a specific past period

content.caption: Figure 3. A 3-day rolling mean (orange) smooths the noisy daily order counts (blue) while tracking the underlying trend.

content.text: A rolling mean summarizes recent history while reducing sudden random variation; a rolling standard deviation shows whether behaviour is stable or volatile.
content.title: Why rolling features help

content.text: The same idea appears across domains:
Aggregation by data type

rows: sum, mean, median, min, max, std
min date, max date, recency, duration

content.text: Aggregating in pandas

content.code:
import pandas as pd

# One row per order
orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "customer_id": ["C01", "C01", "C01", "C02", "C02", "C03"],
    "order_amount": [120, 80, 150, 200, 60, 40],
    "category": ["Electronics", "Books", "Electronics",
                 "Home", "Books", "Books"],
})

customer_features = (
    orders.groupby("customer_id")
          .agg(
              order_count=("order_amount", "count"),
              total_spend=("order_amount", "sum"),
              avg_order_value=("order_amount", "mean"),
              max_order_value=("order_amount", "max"),
              unique_categories=("category", "nunique"),
          )
          .reset_index()
)

print(customer_features)
content.explanation: Named aggregation (output=(column, func)) builds several features in one groupby, one row per customer.

content.text: Rolling aggregation

content.code:
daily_sales["sales_7d_mean"] = (
    daily_sales["sales"]
    .rolling(window=7, min_periods=1)
    .mean()
)

daily_sales["sales_7d_std"] = (
    daily_sales["sales"]
    .rolling(window=7, min_periods=2)
    .std()
)
content.explanation: rolling(window=7) summarizes the last seven rows; sort by time first and, in grouped data, compute per entity.

content.text: Use names that show the metric and window: spend_sum_30d, orders_count_7d, amount_mean_90d. Clear names reduce confusion during modelling.
content.title: Naming rule

content.text: Derived aggregated features
A derived aggregate combines two or more basic summaries into a more meaningful feature:
Important design decisions

items: Correct level of aggregation — match the prediction unit (one row per customer for churn; per product-period for demand).
Appropriate time horizon — fraud may need minutes/hours; loyalty may need months.
Missing groups — an entity with no events may need a zero, not a missing value; it depends on what absence means.
Outliers — a few huge values distort sums and means; consider median, trimmed mean, clipping, or a log transform.
Feature redundancy — total spend, order count, and average order value can strongly overlap.
Consistency at inference — the same grouping, reference dates, filters, and windows must be used in deployment.

content.text: Data leakage: the biggest risk

Data leakage happens when an aggregated feature uses information that would not have been available at prediction time. It makes evaluation look unrealistically good — and then the model fails in production.

content.caption: Figure 4. Valid aggregation uses only events before the prediction date; pulling in later activity (future months) is leakage.

content.text: To predict whether a customer will churn on 31 March, do not calculate total purchases using April or May data. Only events before 31 March may be used.
content.title: Leakage example

content.text: Common mistakes and solutions

rows: Check the primary entity ID and relationship keys
Old and recent behaviour treated equally
Create short-, medium-, and long-term windows
Use safe division; define zero-denominator behaviour
Some models can't handle missing values
Use meaningful zero, imputation, or a missing flag

content.text: Best-practice checklist

items: Define the exact prediction unit.
Choose a clear cutoff date for each observation.
Use only information available before that cutoff.
Create both absolute summaries (sum, count) and normalized ones (mean, rate).
Compare multiple time windows when behaviour changes over time.
Use robust statistics such as the median for strongly skewed data.
Document group keys, filters, window sizes, and missing-value rules.
Recalculate features with the same pipeline during validation and deployment.
Measure whether each new feature improves cross-validated performance.

content.text: Mini practice activity
A delivery company wants to predict whether a driver will be late on the next route. It has one row per completed delivery.

items: Possible group: driver_id.
Possible windows: last 7 days and last 30 days.
Possible features: delivery_count_7d, avg_delay_minutes_30d, max_delay_7d, late_delivery_rate_30d, unique_routes_30d.
Leakage rule: use only deliveries completed before the next-route prediction time.

content.text: Why should late_delivery_rate_30d be computed only from deliveries finished before the prediction moment — and why add both a 7-day and a 30-day window instead of just one?
content.title: Think it through

content.text: Answer

Including the route being predicted (or any later delivery) would leak the outcome into the feature, inflating validation scores and failing in production. Two windows capture different signals: the 7-day window reflects the driver's very recent form, while the 30-day window reflects their stable baseline — together they let the model tell a temporary dip apart from a persistent pattern.
Quick summary

rows: Summarize multiple related rows into useful values.
Count, sum, mean, median, min, max, std, unique count, ratio, recency.
Aggregate by the entity or time window matching the task.
Turns raw events into behavioural patterns models can use.
Future information must never enter historical features.
Clear windows, meaningful names, safe ratios, consistent pipelines.

content.text: Aggregated features turn detailed event histories into compact descriptions of frequency, volume, typical behaviour, variation, and recency. Correct grouping and strict time boundaries are essential.
content.title: Final takeaway

keyPoints: Aggregated features summarize many related records (grouped by an entity or time window) into one value, turning event data into model-ready, one-row-per-unit data.
Core operations are count, sum, mean, median, min, max, std, unique count, ratio/rate, and recency — each answering a different question (frequency, volume, typical size, stability, variety).
Time-based windows (rolling, expanding, recent-history) capture recent vs long-term behaviour and smooth short-term noise; use multiple windows when behaviour changes over time.
The biggest risk is data leakage: aggregate only information available before the prediction cutoff date, and apply the identical grouping/windows at inference.
Combine absolute summaries (sum, count) with normalized ones (mean, rate), use robust stats for skew, guard against divide-by-zero, and validate that each feature helps.
commonMistakes: Aggregating future records (after the prediction cutoff), causing target leakage and over-optimistic evaluation.
Grouping by the wrong key, or ignoring time windows so old and recent behaviour count equally.
Using only sums (which favour large groups) instead of adding normalized means and rates.
Dividing by zero in ratio features, or leaving missing aggregates untreated for entities with no events.

lessons.title: Domain-Based Feature Creation
lessons.summary: How to turn expert knowledge of a field, business process, or scientific rule into meaningful new variables. Covers the definition and how it differs from ordinary transformation, the five-step create-and-validate workflow, where domain knowledge comes from, common patterns (ratio, difference, rate, threshold flag, recency, cumulative, deviation, interaction), and worked examples across healthcare (pulse pressure, BMI, MAP), finance and fraud (debt-to-income, credit utilisation, velocity, personal-baseline features), retail (RFM, average basket value), and predictive maintenance (deviation from baseline). Includes a pandas implementation with divide-by-zero safeguards, evaluation and quality checklists, target-leakage examples, domain-vs-learned features, and a self-check with glossary.

content.text: Teaching the data what it means

Raw data tells you what was recorded; domain knowledge tells you what those numbers mean. A dataset might store monthly income and monthly debt as two separate columns, but a lender knows the real signal is the relationship between them — the debt-to-income ratio. Domain-based feature creation is the craft of turning that expert understanding into new variables, giving the model concepts it would struggle to discover on its own.

content.caption: Figure 1. Finance knowledge turns raw variables (income, debt, credit limit, credit used) into meaningful domain features: debt-to-income ratio 0.30 and credit utilisation 0.75.

content.text: Using knowledge about a specific field, business process, scientific rule, or real-world system to build new variables from existing data. The new variables represent concepts that are meaningful in that domain and may be easier for a model to learn from.
Raw data tells us what was recorded. Domain features express what the recorded values mean in the real-world problem.
content.title: Core idea

content.text: These notes stay focused on domain-based feature creation. Other feature-engineering methods appear only when needed to explain this topic.
content.title: Scope

content.text: A simple example
A bank dataset has monthly income and monthly debt payment. Each is useful, but their relationship is more informative than either alone:

content.expression: Debt-to-income ratio = Monthly debt payment ÷ Monthly income
content.explanation: A higher ratio can indicate that a larger share of income is already committed to debt.

content.text: How it differs from ordinary transformation

rows: Creates a concept based on how the domain works.
Usually needs business, scientific, or medical knowledge.
Goal: improve meaning and predictive signal.

content.text: A feature should not be kept only because it sounds intelligent. It must be logically valid and empirically useful.
content.title: Important

content.text: What you'll be able to do

items: Explain what makes a feature domain-based.
Recognise common domain-feature patterns (ratios, differences, rates, thresholds, recency).
Create domain features across healthcare, finance, retail, and manufacturing.
Avoid target leakage and validate whether a feature genuinely helps.

content.text: The five-step workflow

content.caption: Figure 2. The workflow: understand the domain → identify useful relationships → create domain features → check leakage and validity → evaluate model performance.

items: Understand the prediction problem — what the model predicts, who uses it, and when the prediction is made.
Study the real process — identify ratios, thresholds, cycles, delays, interactions, physical rules, and expert indicators.
Form a hypothesis — explain why a proposed feature could relate to the target.
Create the feature using only information available at prediction time.
Validate it — compare performance, stability, interpretability, and fairness before keeping it.

content.text: Where domain knowledge comes from
Common domain-feature patterns

rows: A × B or a combining rule

content.text: Examples across domains

rows: Pressure difference linked to CV risk
How much credit is being used

content.text: Worked example 1: healthcare
Blood-pressure data usually contains systolic and diastolic measurements. Clinicians also read the difference between them, so it can be created as a domain feature:

content.expression:
Pulse pressure = Systolic − Diastolic
Example: 140 − 85 = 55 mmHg

content.caption: Figure 3. Systolic and diastolic readings rise with age; the created pulse-pressure feature (their difference) widens too. Synthetic values, for illustration only.

content.text: Other useful healthcare features:
Clinical thresholds must come from appropriate medical guidance and local practice — they should not be invented from convenience.
content.title: Caution

content.text: Worked example 2: finance and fraud
Finance ratios express risk relative to capacity or collateral:
Fraud-oriented features often compare current activity to a personal baseline:

rows: A new device can be a risk signal
Personalised abnormality beats a global threshold

content.text: When predicting whether a current transaction is fraudulent, do not use information recorded after the transaction was reviewed or confirmed — that is target leakage.
content.title: Prediction-time rule

content.text: Worked example 3: retail (RFM)
Retail data becomes far more useful when individual transactions are summarised into customer-level behaviour. A popular domain approach is RFM:

rows: Time since the most recent purchase
Number of purchases in a period

content.expression: Average basket value = Total sales value ÷ Number of orders
content.explanation: Combines total sales and order count into a spending-intensity feature.

content.text: Other useful retail features:

items: Customer tenure = current date − first purchase date.
Discount dependency = discounted orders ÷ all orders.
Return rate = returned items ÷ purchased items.
Category diversity = number of unique product categories purchased.
Weekend-shopping share = weekend orders ÷ all orders.

content.text: Worked example 4: predictive maintenance
Sensor values are often meaningful only relative to normal operating conditions. Engineering knowledge turns raw readings into deviation, load, trend, and maintenance features:

rows: Share of planned time actually operating

content.expression: Deviation from baseline = Current reading − Expected normal reading
content.explanation: Large absolute deviations can be stronger warning signals than the raw reading alone.

content.text: Implementation in Python
Domain feature definitions should be agreed before model training. This example builds features for a small customer-credit dataset:

content.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# Ratio features with protection against division by zero
df["debt_to_income"] = df["monthly_debt"] / df["monthly_income"].replace(0, np.nan)
df["credit_utilisation"] = df["credit_used"] / df["credit_limit"].replace(0, np.nan)

# Recency feature
df["days_since_last_payment"] = (
    df["prediction_date"] - df["last_payment_date"]
).dt.days

# Domain threshold flag
df["high_utilisation_flag"] = (df["credit_utilisation"] > 0.80).astype(int)

# Combined risk indicator
df["income_pressure"] = df["debt_to_income"] * df["credit_utilisation"]
content.explanation: replace(0, np.nan) guards ratio features against division by zero; the flag and interaction encode domain rules.

content.text: Implementation rules

items: Handle division by zero and missing values explicitly.
Use the same formula in training, validation, testing, and production.
Fit any learned statistics (e.g. a customer baseline) on training data only.
Record the feature definition, units, valid range, and business meaning.
Test extreme and impossible values before model training.

content.text: Evaluating a domain feature

content.caption: Figure 4. Illustrative validation scores: domain-based features tend to edge out raw and generic-transformation feature sets across domains. Example values — real gains depend on the dataset.

content.text: A domain feature is valuable only when it improves the complete modelling objective. Run it through these checks:

rows: Compare cross-validated metrics with and without it
Check across time periods, groups, and locations
Confirm experts can explain its meaning and direction
Verify all raw inputs arrive before prediction
Test for harmful or unjustified group differences

content.text: Common mistakes

rows: Boundary may have no domain meaning

content.text: A bad feature: “Days until loan default” cannot predict default — it requires knowing that default will happen. A valid alternative: “Days since last successful payment”, which uses information available at prediction time.
content.title: Target-leakage example

content.text: Quality checklist

content.caption: Figure 5. Five checks before using a domain feature: Meaningful, Available, Stable, Safe, and Useful.

rows: Does it have a logical relationship with the target?
Can it be calculated before the prediction is made?
Are formula, units, dates, and missing values handled?
Does it avoid future or outcome-confirmation information?
Does it improve performance on unseen data?
Does it work across time and important subgroups?
Can another person reproduce and explain it?

content.text: Domain vs automatically learned features

rows: Can help when data is limited

content.text: They are usually combined, not treated as replacements — domain features plus learned representations often make the strongest models.
content.title: In practice

content.text: Key highlights

items: Domain-based feature creation converts expert understanding into model-ready variables.
Ratios, rates, differences, recency, thresholds, cumulative values, and deviations are common patterns.
Every feature should have a clear real-world meaning and a testable reason for helping.
Features must use only information available at prediction time.
Correct units, missing-value handling, leakage checks, validation, and documentation are essential.
A simple meaningful feature can beat many complicated but irrelevant ones.

content.text: Domain-based feature creation means teaching the dataset an important concept from the real-world domain before asking the model to learn.
content.title: One-line summary

content.text: Self-check

1. What makes a feature “domain-based”? 2. Why can a ratio be more informative than two raw values? 3. Give one healthcare and one finance example of a domain feature. 4. What is target leakage in domain-feature creation? 5. How would you validate whether a newly created feature is useful? 6. Why must units and prediction time be checked?
content.title: Test yourself

content.text: Answers

items: It encodes a concept from field/process knowledge (a real-world meaning), not just a mathematical transform of a column.
A ratio expresses one quantity relative to another (e.g. debt vs income), capturing burden or intensity that neither raw value shows alone.
Healthcare: pulse pressure (systolic − diastolic) or BMI; Finance: debt-to-income ratio or credit utilisation.
Using information that would not be available when the prediction is made (e.g. outcome-confirmation data), which inflates evaluation.
Compare cross-validated performance with and without it, check stability across groups/time, confirm interpretability and production availability.
Wrong units make ratios/differences meaningless, and a feature that needs future data cannot be computed at prediction time.

content.text: Mini glossary

rows: The specific field or area (healthcare, finance, retail, engineering)
Understanding of rules, processes, risks, and behaviour in that field
A reasoned statement for why a feature may relate to the target
A normal or expected value used for comparison
A boundary used to mark a meaningful condition
Using information unavailable when the prediction is made
Testing whether a feature is correct, stable, and useful on unseen data

keyPoints: Domain-based feature creation converts expert/process knowledge into new variables that carry real-world meaning, unlike ordinary math transforms.
Common patterns are ratios, differences, rates, threshold flags, recency, cumulative measures, deviations from baseline, and interactions.

Worked domains: healthcare (pulse pressure, BMI), finance/fraud (debt-to-income, credit utilisation, personal-baseline velocity), retail (RFM, average basket value), maintenance (deviation from baseline).
Every feature must use only information available at prediction time, handle units/divide-by-zero/missing values, and be applied identically in training and production.
Keep a domain feature only after validating that it improves performance, is stable, interpretable, available in production, and fair — a simple meaningful feature can beat many irrelevant ones.
commonMistakes: Using future or outcome-confirmation information (e.g. “days until default”), causing target leakage.
Inventing arbitrary thresholds instead of using standards, expert evidence, or validation.
Ignoring units or dividing by zero so ratios/differences become inconsistent or invalid.
Creating many hand-made or sensitive-proxy features without clear hypotheses, adding noise or unfairness.

lessons.title: Feature Scaling
lessons.summary: How to transform numerical features onto comparable ranges so no feature dominates a model just because of its unit. Covers the definition and why scaling matters (fair contribution, faster optimization, stable regularization, meaningful distances, numerical stability), the five main methods with formulas and worked examples — standardization (z-score), min-max normalization, MaxAbs, robust scaling, and unit-vector normalization — a comparison table and decision guide, which algorithms are scale-sensitive vs insensitive, the leakage-safe workflow (split first, fit on training only, use a pipeline), scikit-learn code, a two-method worked dataset, common mistakes, scaling vs related transforms, a practical activity, and a self-check.

content.text: Putting features on a level playing field

Imagine a model comparing customers by age (20–60) and annual income (30,000–200,000). To a distance-based algorithm, income looks thousands of times more important than age — not because it carries more information, but simply because its numbers are bigger. Feature scaling fixes this: it transforms numerical features onto comparable ranges or statistical properties so no feature dominates purely by its unit of measurement.

content.caption: Figure 1. Feature-scaling methods at a glance: Standardization (no fixed range), Min-Max ([0,1]), MaxAbs ([-1,1]), Robust (no fixed range), Unit norm (vector length = 1).

content.text: A preprocessing technique that transforms numerical features so they have comparable ranges, magnitudes, or statistical properties. It prevents a feature with large numbers from dominating a model only because of its unit of measurement.
Feature scaling changes the numerical representation of features, not their underlying meaning. Relative ordering and patterns are normally preserved.
content.title: Key idea

content.text: These notes stay focused on feature scaling — why it's needed, how each method works, and how to apply it without data leakage.
content.title: Scope

content.text: What you'll be able to do

items: Define feature scaling and explain its purpose.
Calculate standardized and normalized values by hand.
Compare StandardScaler, MinMaxScaler, MaxAbsScaler, RobustScaler, and unit-vector normalization.
Identify algorithms that are sensitive or insensitive to feature scale.
Apply scaling through a training pipeline and prevent data leakage.

content.text: A simple example
Two features used to predict whether a customer will buy:
Income values are thousands of times larger than age. A distance-based model may treat income as more important even when age is equally informative.

content.caption: Figure 2. Before scaling: income spans tens of thousands while age spans tens, so income dominates the numeric range.
Figure 3. After standardization: age and income sit on comparable z-score units, so both can contribute fairly.

content.text: Why feature scaling matters

items: Fair contribution — features influence the model by information, not numerical magnitude.
Faster optimization — gradient-based algorithms often converge quicker with comparable scales.
Stable regularization — L1 and L2 penalties treat coefficients more fairly after scaling.
Meaningful distances — Euclidean, Manhattan, and cosine calculations become less biased by units.
Better numerical stability — extreme magnitudes can slow calculations or destabilise updates.

content.caption: Figure 4. Before scaling, income accounts for almost all of the squared Euclidean distance; after scaling, age and income contribute far more evenly.

content.text: Scaling does not guarantee better accuracy for every model. It matters most when an algorithm depends on distances, gradients, dot products, variance, or coefficient penalties.
content.title: Important

content.text: The main scaling methods
Standardization (z-score)
Centres a feature around zero and expresses values in units of standard deviation.

content.explanation: The transformed training feature usually has mean 0 and standard deviation 1.

items: Useful for logistic regression, regularized linear regression, SVM, PCA, neural networks, and k-means.
Does not restrict values to a fixed range.
Often suitable for general continuous data; perfect normality is not required.
Can be affected by strong outliers, since mean and std are outlier-sensitive.

content.text: Training ages 20, 30, 40 → mean 30, population SD ≈ 8.16. Then age 20 → z = (20−30)/8.16 = −1.23; age 30 → 0; age 40 → +1.23.
content.title: Worked example

content.text: Min-Max normalization
Maps values to a chosen interval, commonly 0 to 1.

content.explanation: The training minimum becomes 0 and the training maximum becomes 1.

items: Preserves the shape and ordering of the original distribution.
Useful when a bounded input range is preferred.
Sensitive to outliers — one extreme value can compress most observations into a narrow band.
A future value outside the training range may map below 0 or above 1.

content.text: For ages 20, 30, 40 (min 20, max 40): age 20 → 0, age 30 → 0.5, age 40 → 1.
content.title: Worked example

content.text: MaxAbs scaling

content.explanation: Values are normally placed within −1 and 1 without subtracting the mean.

items: Preserves zeros, so it is useful for sparse matrices.
Does not center the data.
Sensitive to large extreme values.

content.text: Robust scaling

content.explanation: IQR is the interquartile range, Q3 − Q1.

items: Uses the median and quartiles instead of the mean and standard deviation.
Less affected by extreme outliers.
Useful for skewed financial, transaction, sensor, and real-estate data.
Reduces the effect of outliers but does not remove them.

content.text: Unit-vector normalization

content.explanation: Each sample vector is scaled to length 1, commonly with the L1 or L2 norm.

items: Applied row-wise to samples, not column-wise to features.
Common in text mining, document vectors, information retrieval, and cosine-similarity tasks.
Emphasizes direction or composition rather than overall magnitude.

content.text: Comparing the methods
The two tables below split a full comparison so every column stays readable on a phone:

content.caption: Figure 5. Decision guide: if features have very different scales and the model uses distance/gradients/regularization, pick RobustScaler for strong outliers, Min-Max for a bounded range, or StandardScaler for general continuous data — always fit on training data only.

content.text: Which algorithms need scaling?
Decision trees and most tree ensembles usually do not require scaling — their split decisions depend on ordering and thresholds, not geometric distance.
content.title: Tree-model exception

content.text: Correct workflow: prevent leakage
Data leakage occurs when information from validation or test data influences training. Scaling leaks when its statistics are computed before the train-test split.
Wrong: compute mean/std/min/max/quartiles on the full dataset, scale all rows, then split. Test-set statistics have already leaked into training.
content.title: Wrong procedure

items: Split the dataset into training and test sets.
Fit the scaler using training features only.
Transform the training features with the fitted scaler.
Transform validation and test features using the same stored training parameters.
For cross-validation, place the scaler inside a pipeline so it is fitted separately in every fold.

content.text: Golden rule: fit on training data; transform training, validation, and test data with the same fitted scaler.
content.title: Golden rule

content.text: Python with scikit-learn

content.code:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.20, random_state=42, stratify=y
)

model = Pipeline([
    ("scaler", StandardScaler()),
    ("classifier", LogisticRegression()),
])

model.fit(X_train, y_train)
test_accuracy = model.score(X_test, y_test)
content.explanation: Inside a pipeline the scaler is fitted only on training data during fit — safe for cross-validation and free of accidental leakage.

content.text: Alternative scalers

content.code:
from sklearn.preprocessing import MinMaxScaler, RobustScaler, MaxAbsScaler

minmax = MinMaxScaler(feature_range=(0, 1))
robust = RobustScaler()
maxabs = MaxAbsScaler()
content.explanation: Swap any of these into the pipeline's "scaler" step depending on the data and model.

content.text: Worked dataset: two methods side by side
The same three records under standardization and min-max scaling (split into two tables sharing the raw Age/Income columns to stay mobile-friendly):
Both methods remove the large numerical gap between age and income. Standardization expresses distance from the mean; min-max expresses relative position between the minimum and maximum.
content.title: Interpretation

content.text: Common mistakes and best practices

rows: Split first, fit on training data
Scale y only when the model needs it

content.text: Standardization can reduce numerical magnitude, but it does not make a skewed feature symmetric. Shape problems need transforms such as log, Box-Cox, or Yeo-Johnson.
content.title: Concept check

content.text: Scaling vs related transformations
Practical activity
Use a dataset with at least two numerical features on different units (age, salary, distance, transaction amount):
