lessons.title: Curse of Dimensionality
lessons.summary: Why adding more features can hurt: the feature space grows exponentially (mᵈ cells), so a fixed sample becomes sparse, distances concentrate (nearest and farthest become similar), and models need more data and computation. Covers the definition and terminology, the exponential-growth geometry, data sparsity and projection illusions, distance concentration and its effect on KNN/clustering, a customer example and the effects on models, which algorithms are most affected, symptoms, feature-engineering solutions (selection, dimensionality reduction, regularization), selection-vs-reduction, a practical workflow, a leakage-safe PCA pipeline in scikit-learn, a text-classification case study, common misconceptions, a glossary, and a self-check.

content.text: When more features make things worse

It feels natural to assume that adding more features gives a model more to learn from. Often the opposite is true. As the number of features grows, the space they define expands so fast that the data spreads thin, distances stop meaning much, and models need far more examples just to keep up. This bundle of problems is the curse of dimensionality — and recognising it is the first step to controlling it.

content.caption: Figure 1. The feature space grows exponentially: dividing each feature into ten intervals needs 10¹ cells in 1D, 10² in 2D, up to 10⁷ in 7D.

content.text: A collection of problems that appear when the number of input features (dimensions) becomes large. As dimensions increase, the feature space expands so quickly that observations become sparse, distances become less informative, and models need more data and computation to learn reliable patterns.
Adding more features does not always add useful information. Too many features can make the data space mostly empty and make learning harder.
content.title: Simple meaning

content.text: These notes stay focused on the curse of dimensionality within feature engineering.
content.title: Scope

content.text: What you'll be able to do

items: Define the curse of dimensionality in simple and technical terms.
Explain why high-dimensional data becomes sparse.
Understand distance concentration and its effect on similarity-based algorithms.
Recognise the practical symptoms of excessive dimensionality.
Select feature-engineering strategies to reduce the problem.

rows: Near/far points become similar in distance
Data needed to learn a stable rule
Required size grows fast with dimensions

content.text: Why dimensionality becomes a curse
Imagine dividing every feature into 10 equal intervals. The number of grid cells to cover explodes:

rows: A square grid already needs a hundred cells
A cube needs a thousand cells
Most cells empty unless the data is huge

content.explanation: If every dimension is divided into m intervals, the total number of cells is m to the power d. This exponential growth is the central geometric reason for the curse.

content.caption: Figure 2. Maintaining equal coverage requires exponentially more observations as dimensionality increases — a straight line on a log scale.

content.text: Data sparsity

In a low-dimensional space, observations can be close enough to form clear clusters or neighbourhoods. In a high-dimensional space, the same number of observations is spread across a vastly larger volume, so those neighbourhoods thin out.

content.caption: Figure 3. In two dimensions, a moderate sample covers the visible space reasonably well.
Figure 4. A 2D projection of 50-dimensional data looks similar, but the picture hides the much greater underlying sparsity — local neighbourhoods are far less reliable.

content.text: A two-dimensional plot of high-dimensional data is only a projection. Points that appear close in the plot may not be close in the original feature space.
content.title: Important

content.text: Distance concentration

Many methods depend on distance — k-nearest neighbours, K-means, hierarchical clustering, kernel methods, and anomaly detection. In high dimensions, distances tend to concentrate: the closest and farthest observations become relatively similar in distance.

content.caption: Figure 5. As dimensions rise, the ratio of nearest to farthest distance climbs toward 1 — near and far become hard to tell apart.

content.text: When the nearest point is almost as far away as the farthest point, the concept of a “nearest neighbour” becomes weak — the algorithm may pick neighbours that are not meaningfully similar.
content.title: Interpretation

content.text: A simple numerical example

A model compares customers using age, annual income, visits per month, average basket value, days since last purchase — plus 95 additional variables. Only a small subset is likely relevant to customer behaviour.

rows: Dense enough for useful patterns; easier to interpret
Sparse space; noise dominates; unstable neighbours
Better balance of information and complexity

content.text: The issue is not simply “many features.” The greatest risk occurs when the number of features is large relative to the number of useful observations, and many features are irrelevant, redundant, noisy, or weakly measured.
content.title: Key lesson

content.text: Effects on models

rows: Fits accidental patterns in many directions
Space needs more observations for coverage

content.text: Algorithms most affected

rows: Depends on meaningful distances and density
Large p vs n raises variance/collinearity
More inputs = more params, more data

content.text: How to recognise the problem

items: The feature count is large versus observations (p close to or greater than n).
Training performance improves after adding features, but validation declines.
Nearest-neighbour results shift strongly when a few features are added/removed.
Clustering results are unstable across seeds, samples, or distance metrics.
Many features have near-zero variance, high missingness, or weak target relationship.
Training and hyperparameter tuning become unnecessarily slow.
Feature importance is spread across many weak or highly correlated variables.

content.text: Feature-engineering solutions

content.caption: Figure 6. A practical workflow: start with many features → remove low-value features (selection) → reduce dimensionality (PCA/autoencoder) → validate with cross-validation.

content.text: Feature selection
Keep the original features but remove those that don't contribute enough value:

items: Filter methods — variance threshold, correlation filtering, chi-square, ANOVA, mutual information.
Wrapper methods — recursive feature elimination, forward/backward selection.
Embedded methods — Lasso, tree-based importance, regularized models.

content.text: Dimensionality reduction
Transform many original features into a smaller set of new features that retain important structure:

items: PCA — orthogonal components preserving maximum variance.
Truncated SVD — useful for sparse matrices such as document-term features.
Autoencoders — neural networks that learn compressed representations.
Feature hashing or embeddings — compact representations for very large categorical/text features.

content.text: Regularization and validation

items: L1 regularization can shrink some coefficients to exactly zero.
L2 regularization reduces coefficient magnitude and controls variance.
Cross-validation estimates whether dimensionality reduction genuinely improves generalization.
All selection and reduction steps must be fitted inside the training fold to prevent leakage.

content.text: Do not run feature selection or PCA on the full dataset before splitting or cross-validation. Fit these steps only on training data, then apply the learned transformation to validation/test data.
content.title: Data-leakage warning

content.text: Selection vs reduction

rows: Only some original variables are useful
Info spread across many correlated variables
Removing a weak feature useful in combination

content.text: Practical workflow

items: Create a baseline model with a simple preprocessing pipeline.
Measure the feature-to-sample ratio; inspect missingness, variance, and correlation.
Remove identifiers, leakage variables, duplicate columns, and near-zero-variance features.
Apply feature selection or dimensionality reduction inside a pipeline.
Compare validation performance, stability, training time, and interpretability.
Choose the smallest feature representation that gives reliable performance.
Evaluate once on the untouched test set.

content.text: Python: safe PCA pipeline
This scales features and applies PCA inside a cross-validated pipeline — preprocessing is learned separately within each training fold, so there is no leakage:

content.code:
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, StratifiedKFold
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

X, y = make_classification(
    n_samples=1200, n_features=100,
    n_informative=12, n_redundant=18, random_state=42,
)

pipeline = Pipeline([
    ("scale", StandardScaler()),
    ("pca", PCA(n_components=0.95)),   # retain 95% variance
    ("model", LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000)),
])

cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
scores = cross_val_score(pipeline, X, y, cv=cv, scoring="accuracy")

print("Mean CV accuracy:", scores.mean())
print("CV standard deviation:", scores.std())
content.explanation: The 100 features (only ~30 informative/redundant) are compressed by PCA inside each fold; compare against a baseline without PCA.

content.text: Compare this pipeline with a baseline that omits PCA. Keep PCA only when it improves validation performance, stability, efficiency, or another project objective.

A bag-of-words representation can create tens of thousands of columns while most document rows contain only a few non-zero values — a classic high-dimensional sparse setting.

rows: Remove very rare and extremely common terms
Train linear SVM or logistic regression

rows: They help only when they add reliable info that outweighs added variance
PCA preserves variance, not necessarily target info — validate
Less distance-dependent, but many irrelevant vars still raise variance/cost
No universal threshold — risk depends on n, signal, sparsity, model
Projections distort distances and can create false separation

content.text: Key highlights

items: The feature space grows exponentially with the number of dimensions.
A fixed number of observations becomes increasingly sparse as dimensions increase.
Distances lose contrast, weakening nearest-neighbour, clustering, and anomaly-detection methods.
High dimensionality can increase overfitting, computation, instability, and data requirements.
The best solution is usually a validated mix of feature cleaning, selection, reduction, regularization, and model choice.
Dimensionality-reduction steps must be learned only from training data.

content.text: Curse of dimensionality is the loss of reliable density, distance, and generalization caused by the exponential expansion of the feature space as the number of features increases.

content.text: Quick glossary

rows: Most regions/entries hold little or no information
Linear projection into fewer variance-preserving components
Dimensions actually needed to describe the main structure
Rule used to measure separation between observations

1. Why does a dataset become sparse when dimensions increase? 2. How does distance concentration affect KNN? 3. What is the difference between feature selection and PCA? 4. Why must PCA be fitted inside a training pipeline? 5. Name three symptoms that dimensionality is harming a model. 6. Why is there no fixed number of features that defines “high dimensionality”?
content.title: Test yourself

content.text: Answers

items: The volume of the feature space grows exponentially while the number of observations stays fixed.
Nearest and farthest distances become relatively similar, so selected neighbours may not be meaningfully close.
Feature selection keeps original variables; PCA creates new components from combinations of variables.
To prevent information from validation or test observations influencing the learned transformation.
Validation decline after adding features, unstable neighbours/clusters, long training time, and many weak/redundant variables.
The risk depends on the feature-to-sample ratio, intrinsic dimensionality, signal strength, sparsity, noise, and algorithm.

keyPoints: The feature space grows as mᵈ (exponentially in the number of dimensions), so a fixed number of observations becomes increasingly sparse.
In high dimensions distances concentrate — nearest and farthest points become similar — which weakens KNN, clustering, kernels, and anomaly detection.
Excessive dimensionality raises overfitting, computation, instability, and the amount of data needed; the real risk is high p relative to n with many irrelevant/redundant features.
Control it with feature cleaning, feature selection (filter/wrapper/embedded), dimensionality reduction (PCA/SVD/autoencoders/embeddings), and regularization.
Fit all selection and reduction steps inside the training pipeline only (leakage), and keep a reduction step only when validation confirms it helps.
commonMistakes: Assuming more features always improve accuracy, or that PCA/tree models automatically remove the problem.
Fitting feature selection or PCA on the full dataset before splitting or cross-validation (leakage).
Trusting a 2D projection to prove clusters exist when projections distort distances.
Treating a fixed feature count (e.g. >100) as the definition of high dimensionality instead of considering the p/n ratio, signal, and sparsity.

lessons.title: Preventing Feature Leakage
lessons.summary: How to stop a model from seeing information at training time that it won't have at prediction time. Covers the definition and why leakage inflates metrics, how it enters a project (fit-before-split vs split-first), and the five main types — target, train-test contamination, temporal, group/entity, and validation leakage — each with examples. Includes target leakage (direct/indirect/proxy), preprocessing leakage with a Pipeline fix, temporal leakage with a shift-before-rolling feature and TimeSeriesSplit, group leakage with GroupKFold, validation/test-set roles and nested CV, safe out-of-fold target encoding and aggregates, a churn case study, a prevention checklist, warning signs, safe design patterns, an end-to-end ColumnTransformer pipeline, and a self-check.

content.text: The bug that hides in plain sight

Feature leakage is the most dangerous mistake in machine learning precisely because it doesn't look like a mistake. The code runs, the metrics soar, everyone celebrates — and then the model collapses in production. The cause is almost always the same: during training the model saw information it will never actually have at prediction time. Preventing leakage is less about clever algorithms and more about disciplined data design.

When a model receives information during training that would not be available at the moment the prediction must be made. The hidden information may come from the target, future events, the validation/test set, or other records belonging to the same person or group.
A feature is safe only when it can be calculated at prediction time using information that is genuinely available at that time.
content.title: Core idea

content.text: These notes stay focused on feature leakage and its prevention across features, validation, preprocessing, time-based data, and production workflows.
content.title: Scope

content.text: What you'll be able to do

items: Define feature leakage and explain why it produces misleading performance.
Recognise target leakage, train-test contamination, temporal, group, and validation leakage.
Prevent leakage during preprocessing, feature engineering, cross-validation, and tuning.
Use scikit-learn Pipeline, GroupKFold, and TimeSeriesSplit correctly.
Apply a practical leakage audit before deployment.

content.text: Why leakage is dangerous

items: It makes validation/test scores look better than the model will really perform.
It encourages choosing the wrong features, model, and hyperparameters.
It stays hidden — the code runs successfully and metrics look impressive.
It often causes a large performance drop after deployment.
It reduces trust and can create costly or unsafe decisions.

content.caption: Figure 1. Leaky validation reports 98% accuracy, correct validation 85%, and the real-world test 83% — leakage inflates the reported number far above reality.

content.text: How leakage enters a project

content.caption: Figure 2. Unsafe workflow: fit the scaler/encoder on all data, then split → over-optimistic score. Safe workflow: split first, fit preprocessing on training data only, transform the rest → honest estimate.

content.text: The safest general order: define the prediction moment → split the data → fit preprocessing on training data only → train the model → evaluate once on untouched data.
content.title: The safe order

content.text: The main types of leakage

content.caption: Figure 3. Common sources of leakage by relative risk: target-derived features (95), future-time information (90), preprocessing before split (85), repeated tuning on the test set (80), duplicate/group overlap (75). Illustrative scale.

rows: A feature directly/indirectly reveals the target
Val/test info used in training or preprocessing
Split first; fit transforms on training only
Future info used to predict an earlier event
Same entity's rows in both train and test
Repeated decisions made using the test set
Keep a separate validation set; use test once
Aggregate uses rows outside the allowed window

content.text: Target leakage
Target leakage happens when an input feature carries information strongly tied to the outcome — because the feature was created after the outcome, or from the outcome itself.

rows: Written after the outcome period begins

items: Direct leakage — the feature explicitly contains the target (e.g. “default_status” when predicting default).
Indirect leakage — the feature is a later action caused by the target (e.g. “collection_call_made” when predicting missed payments).
Proxy leakage — the feature is almost equivalent to the target (e.g. “claim_paid_amount” when predicting claim approval).

content.text: Diagnostic question: was this value created before or after the event I am trying to predict? If after, it is probably leakage.
content.title: The key question

content.text: Preprocessing leakage

Many preprocessing steps learn from data — the mean, standard deviation, median, category frequencies, selected features, principal components, imputation values. If these are learned from the complete dataset, validation/test information leaks into training.

rows: Fit scaler on all rows, then split
Split first; fit on training rows only
Learn median from training; apply to test
Select using all labels before CV
Fit PCA on the full dataset
Fit PCA inside a pipeline on the fold's training data
Out-of-fold encoding or a nested pipeline
Apply SMOTE only to each training fold

content.code:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.20, stratify=y, random_state=42
)

safe_model = Pipeline([
    ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
    ("scaler", StandardScaler()),
    ("model", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)),
])

safe_model.fit(X_train, y_train)
test_score = safe_model.score(X_test, y_test)
content.explanation: During cross-validation the pipeline fits the imputer and scaler separately inside each training fold; the validation fold is transformed but never used to learn preprocessing values.

content.text: Temporal leakage

Temporal leakage is common in forecasting, fraud detection, churn, predictive maintenance, finance, and healthcare. It occurs when data from the future is used to build a feature for an earlier prediction.

content.caption: Figure 4. Temporal leakage: a feature built from May/June data is used to predict an April outcome. Rule — every feature must be computable using only information available at prediction time.

content.text: Safe time-based feature engineering

items: Use only records with timestamps at or before the prediction cutoff time.
Use lagged values (yesterday's sales) rather than tomorrow's.
Create rolling averages using past windows only — in pandas, shifting before rolling is often necessary.
Use TimeSeriesSplit or walk-forward validation instead of random cross-validation.
Store feature timestamps and verify feature_time <= prediction_time for every row.

content.code:
# Data must be sorted by customer and time
orders = orders.sort_values(["customer_id", "order_date"])

# Shift first so the current purchase is not included
orders["past_30d_mean"] = (
    orders.groupby("customer_id")["amount"]
          .transform(lambda s: s.shift(1).rolling(30, min_periods=1).mean())
)
content.explanation: shift(1) drops the current row before rolling, so the feature never sees the event it is helping to predict.

content.text: Group and entity leakage

Random row splitting is unsafe when several rows belong to the same entity. A model may memorize entity-specific patterns and appear to generalize, even though it has already seen that entity during training.

content.code:
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold, cross_val_score

cv = GroupKFold(n_splits=5)
scores = cross_val_score(
    safe_model, X, y,
    groups=customer_id, cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc",
)
content.explanation: GroupKFold keeps all rows for a given customer_id inside a single fold, so no entity spans train and validation.

content.text: Validation and test-set leakage
The test set represents unseen future data. It becomes part of training whenever it is checked repeatedly and used to choose features, models, thresholds, or hyperparameters.
A test set is no longer a true test set after its results influence development decisions.
content.title: Important

content.text: For small datasets or intensive tuning, nested cross-validation gives a stronger estimate: the inner loop chooses hyperparameters, the outer loop estimates generalization.
content.title: Nested cross-validation

content.text: Leakage in target encoding and aggregates
Target encoding replaces a category with the average target value for that category — highly useful but dangerous, because each row's label can leak into its own encoded value.

rows: Test targets unused, but training overfit may remain
Each row encoded using other folds, not its own target

content.text: Aggregated features carry the same risk:

items: Customer lifetime value must use only purchases before the prediction date.
Store-level averages must be computed inside training folds, not once on the full dataset.
Counts like “number of complaints” must stop at the prediction cutoff time.
A rolling feature should not include the current row when the current event is part of the outcome.

content.text: Mini case study: customer churn
Goal: on 1 June, predict whether a customer will leave during June. The system may use information available up to 31 May only. Judging candidate features:
A correct evaluation design:

items: Train on customers observed before the chosen historical cutoff.
Create every feature as a snapshot at its own cutoff date.
Validate on a later time period.
Keep customers from the same household/business group in one split when appropriate.
Do not use June events in features used to predict June churn.

content.text: Prevention checklist

rows: Can the exact time of prediction be stated?
Is every feature available at that moment?
Was raw data split before learned preprocessing?
Are imputation, scaling, selection, PCA, modeling in one pipeline?
Are future rows excluded from training and features?
Can the same entity appear in more than one split?
Do duplicates/augmented copies cross split boundaries?
Are stats based only on allowed rows and past windows?
Do any columns reveal the outcome or post-outcome actions?
Was the test set used only after decisions were finalized?
Can the same features be generated in deployment?

content.text: Warning signs of leakage

items: Validation accuracy is unexpectedly close to 100% on a difficult real-world task.
One feature has extremely high importance and its meaning is unclear.
Performance collapses when testing on a later time period or new entity group.
A random split performs much better than a time-based or group-based split.
The deployed system cannot calculate some features used during training.
A column was created after the target event (resolution code, final status, follow-up action).
Model performance changes sharply after removing duplicates.

content.text: Safe design patterns

rows: Split raw data first; use Pipeline / ColumnTransformer
Out-of-fold encoding; fit mappings on training folds only
Resample only the training fold (imbalanced-learn pipeline)
Put selection inside the pipeline, not before CV
Evaluate once on an untouched holdout set

content.text: End-to-end safe example

content.code:
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score

numeric_features = ["age", "income", "tenure"]
categorical_features = ["region", "plan_type"]

numeric_pipe = Pipeline([
    ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
    ("scaler", StandardScaler()),
])
categorical_pipe = Pipeline([
    ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
    ("encoder", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore")),
])

preprocessor = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", numeric_pipe, numeric_features),
    ("cat", categorical_pipe, categorical_features),
])

model = Pipeline([
    ("preprocess", preprocessor),
    ("classifier", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)),
])

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.20, stratify=y, random_state=42
)
cv_scores = cross_val_score(model, X_train, y_train, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc")
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
final_test_auc = model.score(X_test, y_test)
content.explanation: Everything — imputation, scaling, encoding, modeling — lives in one pipeline fitted per fold. For time-based or grouped data, swap in TimeSeriesSplit or GroupKFold.

rows: Use of information unavailable at real prediction time
Split first; learn preprocessing only from training data
Split by group or entity ID

Once, after all modeling decisions are fixed

items: Kuhn, M. & Johnson, K. (2019). Feature Engineering and Selection. CRC Press.

keyPoints: Feature leakage is a data-design and evaluation error: a feature is only safe if it can be computed at prediction time from genuinely available information.

The five types are target leakage (feature reveals the outcome), train-test contamination (preprocessing fit before split), temporal (future info), group/entity (same entity in train and test), and validation (reusing the test set).
Split the raw data first and fit every learned transformation (scaling, imputation, selection, PCA, target encoding) inside the training fold via a Pipeline.
Use TimeSeriesSplit/point-in-time features for time data, GroupKFold for repeated entities, and out-of-fold encoding for target encoding.
Treat suspiciously high validation scores as a reason to investigate, protect the test set for a single final evaluation, and confirm every feature is reproducible in production.

Including post-outcome or target-derived columns (resolution code, days-until-event) as features.

Reusing the test set to tune features/hyperparameters, or encoding a category with its own row's target.

lessons.title: Using Pipelines for Feature Engineering
lessons.summary: How to bundle every feature-engineering step and the model into one scikit-learn object that is reproducible, leakage-safe, and deployable. Covers the definition and why pipelines matter (leakage prevention, reproducibility, deployment, joint tuning), the main components, basic Pipeline and make_pipeline syntax, ColumnTransformer for mixed numeric/categorical data with handle_unknown='ignore', an end-to-end churn example, how pipelines prevent leakage (split-first vs fit-before-split), cross-validation and GridSearchCV with double-underscore parameter naming, custom feature engineering with FunctionTransformer and a BaseEstimator/TransformerMixin class, common mistakes and a best-practice checklist, saving/loading with joblib, and a revision sequence with glossary.

content.text: One object, from raw data to prediction

By now you've met a dozen feature-engineering techniques — imputing, scaling, encoding, transforming, selecting. In a real project these steps stack up, and doing them by hand invites two problems: subtle data leakage, and code that's almost impossible to reproduce or deploy. A pipeline solves both. It bundles every transformation and the final model into a single object that learns from the training data and applies exactly the same rules to everything else.

content.caption: Figure 1. An end-to-end pipeline: raw data → train/test split → preprocessing → feature creation → feature selection → model, all in one reproducible workflow where each CV fold learns preprocessing from its own training portion.

content.text: An ordered sequence of data transformations followed by an estimator. It lets preprocessing, feature engineering, and model training behave as one combined object.
The pipeline learns every required transformation from the training data and then applies the same learned rules to validation, test, and future data.
content.title: Key idea

content.text: These notes stay focused on using pipelines to organize, automate, and safely evaluate feature-engineering steps.
content.title: Scope

content.text: What you'll be able to do

items: Define a pipeline and explain why it helps feature engineering.
Build sequential workflows with scikit-learn Pipeline.
Apply different transformations to different column types with ColumnTransformer.
Prevent data leakage during training and cross-validation.
Tune feature-engineering and model parameters together with GridSearchCV.
Create reproducible training and prediction workflows.

content.text: A pipeline for churn prediction might chain these steps, ending in the estimator:

rows: Fill missing numeric values from training stats
Put numeric features on a comparable scale
Keep the most useful engineered features
Train the classifier on the transformed features

content.text: Why pipelines matter

rows: Transformers fit inside each training fold, not the whole dataset
The same ordered transforms run every train and predict
One object replaces many separate fit/transform/predict calls
Preprocessing travels with the model, never forgotten
Feature-engineering settings and model hyperparameters optimize together
Different preprocessing + model combos share one interface

content.text: Manual vs pipeline workflow

rows: All steps connected in one ordered object
Easy to preprocess test data with full-data stats
Fit occurs only on training data when used correctly
The original table is passed straight to fit/predict
The saved pipeline holds preprocessing + estimator
Parameters use step-name syntax and tune together

content.caption: Figure 2. Illustrative validation scores across folds: the manual workflow (blue) swings widely while the pipeline workflow (orange) is more consistent. Pipelines improve consistency and reduce leakage — they don't guarantee a higher score.

content.text: Main components

items: Transformer — learns with fit() and changes data with transform() (SimpleImputer, StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder).
Estimator — the final model that learns from engineered features (LogisticRegression, RandomForestClassifier).
Step name — a unique label for each stage, used when accessing or tuning parameters.
Sequential execution — the output of one transformer is the input of the next.
Final prediction — after all transforms, the final estimator produces predictions.

content.text: All intermediate steps must support transform(). The final step only needs fit() and usually predict() or predict_proba().
content.title: Important

content.caption: Figure 3. A pipeline can expand then reduce the feature count: 6 raw → 14 after encoding → 28 after interactions → 10 after selection. Example only — exact counts depend on the data.

content.text: Basic Pipeline syntax
This scales numeric features, selects the useful ones, and trains logistic regression:

content.code:
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest, f_classif
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

pipeline = Pipeline(steps=[
    ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
    ("scaler", StandardScaler()),
    ("selector", SelectKBest(score_func=f_classif, k=5)),
    ("model", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)),
])

pipeline.fit(X_train, y_train)
y_pred = pipeline.predict(X_test)
content.explanation: Each named step learns from the training data in order; fit() chains them, and predict() re-applies the fitted transforms to X_test.

content.text: How the code runs, step by step:

items: The imputer learns medians from X_train and fills missing values.
The scaler learns means and standard deviations from the imputed training features.
SelectKBest scores the scaled training features and keeps the chosen subset.
LogisticRegression trains on the final engineered feature matrix.
On predict(), X_test passes through the fitted imputer, scaler, and selector before prediction.

content.text: make_pipeline()
A shorter alternative that generates step names automatically from class names:

content.code:
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

pipeline = make_pipeline(
    SimpleImputer(strategy="median"),
    StandardScaler(),
    LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000),
)
content.explanation: Pipeline() gives explicit step names; make_pipeline() is shorter but auto-names steps (simpleimputer, standardscaler, logisticregression).

content.text: ColumnTransformer for mixed data
Real datasets contain numeric, categorical, text, and date columns — each needing different feature engineering. ColumnTransformer applies separate branches and combines their outputs.

content.caption: Figure 4. ColumnTransformer routes each column group through its own branch — numeric (median + scaler), categorical (most-frequent + one-hot), text/date (custom) — then combines them into one feature matrix for the model.

content.code:
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

numeric_features = ["age", "income", "account_balance"]
categorical_features = ["city", "job_type"]

numeric_pipeline = Pipeline(steps=[
    ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
    ("scaler", StandardScaler()),
])
categorical_pipeline = Pipeline(steps=[
    ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
    ("encoder", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore")),
])

preprocessor = ColumnTransformer(transformers=[
    ("num", numeric_pipeline, numeric_features),
    ("cat", categorical_pipeline, categorical_features),
])

full_pipeline = Pipeline(steps=[
    ("preprocessor", preprocessor),
    ("model", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)),
])

full_pipeline.fit(X_train, y_train)
y_pred = full_pipeline.predict(X_test)
content.explanation: Numeric and categorical columns each get their own imputer/transform branch; ColumnTransformer concatenates the results for the model.

content.text: A new category may appear in validation, test, or production. With handle_unknown="ignore", the encoder represents the unseen category with zeros across the known columns rather than failing — though important unexpected categories should still be monitored.
content.title: Why handle_unknown='ignore' helps

rows: Controls sparse vs dense combined output

content.text: End-to-end example: churn
Problem: predict whether a customer will leave a service. The dataset has missing values plus numerical and categorical variables.

content.code:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report

X = df.drop(columns="churn")
y = df["churn"]

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.20, random_state=42, stratify=y
)

full_pipeline.fit(X_train, y_train)
predictions = full_pipeline.predict(X_test)

print(classification_report(y_test, predictions))
content.explanation: The same full_pipeline handles imputation, scaling, encoding, and modeling for a new customer record passed straight to predict().

content.text: Pipelines and data leakage
Data leakage occurs when information from validation or test data influences training, producing over-optimistic results and weaker real-world performance.

content.code:
# Incorrect: scaler learns from the complete dataset
X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X_scaled, y, test_size=0.20, random_state=42
)
content.explanation: Fitting the scaler on all of X before splitting lets test-set statistics leak into training.

content.code:
# Correct: split first, then fit preprocessing inside the pipeline
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.20, random_state=42
)

pipeline.fit(X_train, y_train)
y_pred = pipeline.predict(X_test)
content.explanation: Splitting first and fitting the pipeline on X_train only keeps every learned statistic inside the training data.

rows: Imputer learns only from the training fold
Scaler fitted only after the training subset is chosen
Features chosen using all rows' targets
Selection repeats inside every training fold
Components learned from the full dataset
PCA learned only from training data
Encodings computed within training data only

content.text: Any transformation that learns from data should be fitted after splitting and included inside the cross-validation pipeline.
content.title: Rule to remember

content.text: Cross-validation and tuning
Because a pipeline behaves like one estimator, it can be passed directly to cross-validation functions:

content.code:
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

scores = cross_val_score(full_pipeline, X, y, cv=5, scoring="accuracy")
print(scores)
print(scores.mean())
content.explanation: cross_val_score refits the whole pipeline inside each of the 5 folds, so preprocessing never sees the validation fold.

content.text: Naming nested parameters
Pipeline parameters use double underscores: step_name__parameter_name. Nested components need multiple levels:

rows: C of the final logistic regression model
Imputation strategy in the numeric branch
Frequency threshold in the categorical encoder
Number of features kept by SelectKBest

content.text: GridSearchCV example

content.code:
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV

parameter_grid = {
    "preprocessor__num__imputer__strategy": ["mean", "median"],
    "model__C": [0.1, 1.0, 10.0],
}

search = GridSearchCV(
    estimator=full_pipeline, param_grid=parameter_grid,
    cv=5, scoring="accuracy", n_jobs=-1,
)

search.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(search.best_params_)
best_pipeline = search.best_estimator_
content.explanation: GridSearchCV refits the complete sequence in each fold, so feature-engineering and model settings are evaluated together without leaking fold information.

content.text: Custom feature engineering
Not every useful transformation has a ready-made class. Custom feature engineering can still live inside a pipeline via FunctionTransformer or a custom transformer class.
FunctionTransformer

content.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import FunctionTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline

log_transformer = FunctionTransformer(
    np.log1p, feature_names_out="one-to-one"
)

numeric_pipeline = Pipeline(steps=[
    ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
    ("log", log_transformer),
    ("scaler", StandardScaler()),
])
content.explanation: FunctionTransformer wraps a stateless function (here log1p) so it slots into the pipeline like any other step.

content.text: Custom transformer class

content.explanation: Inheriting BaseEstimator/TransformerMixin makes it pipeline-compatible; note the copy() and the divide-by-zero guard.

content.text: Requirements for a custom transformer:

items: Inherit from BaseEstimator and TransformerMixin for scikit-learn compatibility.
Put configuration in __init__ without data-dependent calculations there.
Use fit() to learn any training statistics and return self.
Use transform() to return the modified feature matrix.
Avoid changing the input in place — create a safe copy.
Handle missing values, zero denominators, and unexpected input types carefully.

content.text: Common mistakes and best practices

rows: Split first; fit the pipeline on training data
Use the same fitted pipeline for both
Use named columns; preserve the schema
Prediction fails on a new category
Place the selector inside the pipeline
A custom transformer that mutates X
Copy the input before changing columns

content.text: Best-practice checklist

items: Split before fitting any data-dependent transformer.
Use ColumnTransformer for mixed types instead of manually joining arrays.
Give steps clear names (numeric_preprocessing, feature_selection, model).
Use random_state where supported for reproducibility.
Inspect generated feature names when debugging encoded/selected features.
Evaluate the complete pipeline with cross-validation, not just the final model.
Tune preprocessing and estimator hyperparameters together.
Save the complete fitted pipeline with joblib or similar.
Validate expected input columns, types, and category behaviour before deployment.
Document custom features so their business meaning stays clear.

content.text: Saving and loading

content.code:
import joblib

# Save
joblib.dump(best_pipeline, "customer_churn_pipeline.joblib")

# Load and predict
loaded_pipeline = joblib.load("customer_churn_pipeline.joblib")
new_predictions = loaded_pipeline.predict(new_customer_data)
content.explanation: A saved pipeline applies exactly the same feature engineering used during training before every production prediction.

A mini worked sequence for any tabular project:

items: Identify numeric, categorical, and other feature groups.
Build a transformer pipeline for each group.
Combine them with ColumnTransformer.
Optionally add feature creation, reduction, or selection steps.
Add the final estimator as the last step.
Split the data and fit the pipeline on training data only.
Evaluate the complete pipeline using test data and cross-validation.
Tune nested parameters and save the best fitted pipeline.

Yes — before the estimator, so it runs inside each fold

content.text: A strong pipeline is not just cleaner code — it is a control mechanism that keeps feature engineering consistent, repeatable, and correctly separated between training and evaluation data.

Applies a learned transformation to data

It applies different transformations to different column groups (numeric vs categorical) and combines them; a single Pipeline applies the same steps to every column.
model__C — the step name, double underscore, then the parameter name.

keyPoints: A pipeline is an ordered sequence of transformers followed by an estimator; it learns transformations from training data and reapplies them to validation, test, and production data.
Pipelines prevent leakage by fitting every data-dependent step inside each training fold, and they make workflows reproducible and directly deployable.
ColumnTransformer applies different branches to numeric, categorical, and other column groups and combines the outputs; use handle_unknown='ignore' for unseen categories.

lessons.title: Practical Activity: Improve a Model with Better Features
lessons.summary: The Module 8 capstone — a full worked activity that improves a telecom churn model by creating and selecting better features while keeping the algorithm fixed. Walks through preparing and splitting data, training a logistic-regression baseline, creating ratio/threshold/indicator/interaction features (support_intensity, charges_per_product, is_new_customer, month_contract_high_charge), selecting the top features with mutual information on training data only, and comparing baseline vs engineered vs selected models on the same held-out test set (with a metric-comparison table, random-forest importance, and confusion matrices). Includes how to interpret the metric changes, a decision principle, common mistakes, a practical checklist, a loan-default practice task, and a summary — emphasising fair comparison, no leakage, and production availability.

content.text: Putting the whole module to work

This is where every idea in Module 8 comes together. You'll take a raw dataset, build a plain baseline model, engineer better features by hand, select the strongest ones without leaking the target, and then prove — with a fair, identical test set — whether the changes actually helped. Same algorithm throughout; only the features change. That discipline is exactly how real feature-engineering work is judged.

content.caption: Figure 1. The end-to-end workflow for this activity: prepare data → train baseline → create features → select features → retrain & compare on the same test set.

content.text: Transforming raw variables into more informative inputs, removing weak or redundant inputs, retraining the model, and checking whether the change improves performance on unseen data.
This note stays focused on one task: improving a model by creating useful features, selecting the strongest features, and comparing performance fairly.

Create ratio, indicator, threshold, and interaction features.

content.text: Why this activity matters

items: Many algorithms cannot automatically discover every useful ratio, threshold, or interaction from raw data.
A small set of meaningful features may outperform a large set of noisy features.
Better features can improve accuracy, recall, and interpretability without changing the algorithm.

content.caption: Figure 2. Raw customer fields (tenure, support calls, monthly charges, products, contract) are converted into model-ready signals (support_intensity, charges_per_product, is_new_customer, interaction flags) that express risk more directly.

content.text: The worked problem

A telecom company wants to predict which customers may cancel. The target is churn — a customer who leaves is 1, a customer who stays is 0. The example uses 1,500 synthetic records; the metrics are illustrative but come from a real model run. A sample of the raw data (all five shown customers stayed, churn = 0), split so every column stays readable on a phone:
The core question: can the same logistic-regression algorithm perform better when the data is represented with more meaningful features?
content.title: The question

content.text: Step 1 — prepare the data

items: Separate the target (churn) from the input features.
Split into training and test sets before any feature selection.
Use stratification so both sets have a similar churn proportion.
One-hot encode categorical variables (contract type, payment method).
Standardize numeric inputs for logistic regression.

content.code:
X = data.drop(columns=['churn'])
y = data['churn']

train_idx, test_idx = train_test_split(
    np.arange(len(data)), test_size=0.25,
    random_state=42, stratify=y,
)
content.explanation: Splitting the row indices with stratify=y keeps the churn rate consistent across train and test.

content.text: Never use the test set to decide which features to create, keep, or remove. The test set is only for the final unbiased comparison.
content.title: Important rule

content.text: Step 2 — train a baseline
Train a simple model using only the original fields to establish a starting point. Logistic regression is used here because it is fast, interpretable, and suited to binary classification.
Step 3 — create better features
Create features that express customer behaviour more directly than the raw fields. Each must have a clear reason and be computable at real prediction time.

rows: Frequent support need vs normal contact
How heavily each product is used
An interaction raw fields may hide

content.code:
X['support_intensity'] = (
    X['support_calls'] / np.sqrt(X['tenure_months'] + 1)
)
X['charges_per_product'] = (
    X['monthly_charges'] / X['num_products']
)
X['is_new_customer'] = (X['tenure_months'] <= 6).astype(int)
X['month_contract_high_charge'] = (
    (X['contract_type'] == 'Month-to-month') &
    (X['monthly_charges'] > 75)
).astype(int)
content.explanation: Ratios use +1 or sqrt guards to avoid division blow-ups; flags become 0/1 with .astype(int).

content.text: Step 4 — retrain with engineered features
Use the same training records, test records, algorithm, and metrics — only the input representation changes. This isolates the effect of feature engineering.
Step 5 — select the strongest features
Feature selection is done on the training set using mutual information, which measures whether knowing a feature reduces uncertainty about the target. The top 13 features are kept:

content.code:
scores = mutual_info_classif(X_train, y_train, random_state=42)
ranked = pd.Series(scores, index=X_train.columns).sort_values(ascending=False)
selected_features = ranked.head(13).index

model.fit(X_train[selected_features], y_train)
content.explanation: mutual_info_classif is computed on X_train only; the model then trains on just the top-13 columns.

content.text: A feature can score highly and still be invalid if it contains future information, target information, or anything unavailable at prediction time.
content.title: Selection warning

content.text: Results and comparison
All three models are scored on the same held-out test set. The comparison is split into two tables to stay mobile-friendly:

Figure 5. Confusion matrices: the selected-feature model correctly keeps more true 'stay' customers (209 vs 199) while holding churn detection steady — fewer false churn alerts.

A model can look strong while missing most positives
A feature is useless if unavailable at prediction time

content.text: Practical checklist

items: Define the target and prediction time clearly.
Split the data before feature selection.
Train a baseline model.
Create features with a logical or domain-based reason.
Check missing values, extreme values, and division by zero.
Remove leakage and duplicate information.
Select features on training data only.
Retrain using the same algorithm and split.
Compare several metrics, not only accuracy.
Document each feature formula so it can be reproduced.

content.title: Final takeaway

content.text: You engineer a feature that lifts test accuracy by 0.05, but it can only be computed three days after the prediction is due. Should you keep it — and what single principle settles the question?
content.title: Test your judgement

content.text: Answer

No — discard it. A feature must be computable using information available at prediction time; a value that only exists days later cannot be used in production, no matter how much it improves an offline score. Deployability and leakage-safety override raw metric gains every time.

keyPoints: Improve a model by creating more informative features and selecting the strongest ones — keep the algorithm, split, and metrics fixed so the experiment is fair.
Always train a baseline first, then create domain-informed ratios, thresholds, indicators, and interactions, each with a clear reason and computable at prediction time.
Select features on the training set only (e.g. mutual information); using the test set to choose features leaks information and inflates results.
Compare several metrics on the same held-out test set — not every metric must rise (here accuracy/precision/F1 improve while ROC-AUC dips slightly), which is a genuine trade-off.
Keep an engineered feature only if it improves validated performance, stays understandable, avoids leakage, and can be computed reliably in production.
commonMistakes: Selecting or creating features using the test set (or target/future information), causing leakage and optimistic scores.
Adding many meaningless feature combinations that add noise, overfitting, and maintenance cost.
Comparing models on different test records or judging only by accuracy instead of several metrics.
Keeping a high-scoring feature that cannot actually be computed at prediction time in production.
